<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Stressful life events (SLEs) are established precursors to adverse geriatric outcomes; however, their association with hip fracture risk and underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study evaluated the association between SLEs and incident hip fracture among Chinese older adults, specifically examining depressive symptoms as a potential intermediary pathway.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this prospective cohort study, we utilized data from 3,706 participants (aged ≥ 65 years) from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). SLEs were quantified across five key adulthood domains. Incident hip fractures were ascertained through standardized self-reports. Time-to-event outcomes were analyzed using multivariable Cox regression and exploratory mediation analysis for depressive symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Over a 9-year follow-up, 218 (5.9%) participants sustained a hip fracture. Cumulative SLEs exhibited a dose-dependent association with fracture risk (HR = 1.32; 95% CI: 1.13–1.54 per additional event). Compared with no SLEs, adjusted HRs were 1.57 (95% CI: 1.07–2.31) for one event and 2.14 (95% CI: 1.43–3.20) for ≥ 2 events. In an exploratory mediation analysis, depressive symptoms accounted for 11.4% of the association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cumulative SLEs are associated with hip fracture risk in a dose-dependent manner among older Chinese adults, with depressive symptoms potentially serving as an intermediary pathway. These findings support the consideration of integrating psychosocial assessments into fracture prevention strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Stressful life events and hip fracture risk in older Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The risk of sarcopenia is associated with dysregulation of the heart‑brain‑muscle network. This study investigated whether elastic band resistance training (RT) modulates these integrative pathways. Forty older women (mean age 76.4 ± 5.8 years, Ishii score ≥ 120) were randomly assigned to a control group (CON; health education) or an RT group (health education plus 12 weeks of RT). Muscle mass, muscle strength, physical function, gait parameters, skeletal muscle and cardiac morphology, and corticomuscular coherence (CMC) were assessed at baseline and after 12 weeks. RT significantly improved muscle strength and physical function (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.05) and reduced the Ishii score (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.01). Gait analysis showed increased stride length (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.01) and reduced double‑support time (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.01). Ultrasound examination revealed significant increases in biceps brachii thickness, rectus femoris cross‑sectional area, rectus femoris pennation angle, interventricular septal thickness (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.05), as well as in LVEF and E/A ratio (
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.01). After correction for multiple comparisons, the β‑band coherence areas for the vastus lateralis and biceps femoris increased (adjusted
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.05). RT reduced sarcopenia risk and was associated with improvements in physical function, gait stability, and corticomuscular coherence, as well as changes in selected cardiac indices. These findings suggest parallel adaptations rather than directly demonstrating integrated regulation of the heart‑brain‑muscle network.
                  </jats:p>
title: Elastic band resistance training improves physical function, gait, cardiac indices, and corticomuscular coherence in older women at risk of sarcopenia: a randomized controlled trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Different criteria were developed to identify drugs with a negative benefit/risk ratio in older adults, so-called potentially inappropriate medication (PIM). We investigated the correlation between the number of PIMs identified using PRISCUS 2.0, STOPP version 3, and Beers criteria and the functional and nutritional status of Turkish geriatric patients, as assessed by comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective cross-sectional analysis was conducted in geriatric outpatients over the past 10 months. Data were collected on age, clinical conditions, medication, and CGA test results. To identify independent factors associated with PIM use and to adjust for potential confounding, logistic regression analyses were performed. PIM use was analysed as a binary outcome (no PIM versus at least one PIM), and no imputation was performed. Two logistic regression models were fitted in 362 patients with complete data, without (Model 1) and with (Model 2) the number of drugs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 397 participants, 58.7% (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 233) of patients received at least one PIM when combining all three criteria (PIM-ALL). Multivariable analyses showed that the number of medications and functional status (Katz Activities of Daily Living) were most strongly associated with PIM use. In the fully adjusted model (Model 2,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 362), each additional medication was associated with 55% higher odds of PIM use (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.40–1.73), while a higher Katz ADL score was associated with lower odds (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.60–0.87).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>There is relevant variability among PIM tools and in their association with CGA test results. Advanced, systematic, and easily implementable methodologies are required to address these shortcomings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study does not involve a clinical trial and thus was not registered.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association between inappropriate medications and comprehensive geriatric assessment outcomes: a cross-sectional study using PRISCUS, STOPP, and Beers criteria

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To improve the situation of informal caregivers, both supportive efforts for caregiver and rehabilitation for the person with dementia, may be needed. This randomized controlled pilot trial evaluated, among caregivers, the feasibility of a person-centred multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for community-dwelling people with dementia that incorporated an education and support intervention for informal caregivers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Informal caregivers were randomized alongside the person with dementia to an intervention group (n=36) or usual care (n=31). Multiprofessional team rehabilitation for individuals with dementia and support for caregivers, were offered for one 20-week and two 4-week follow-up periods after 5 and 14 months. Caregivers were offered assessments, participation in group sessions, and individual support. After the last group session, scheduled during the last four weeks of the 20-week period, a survey was distributed. Attendance at group sessions and uptake of individual support were recorded. Blinded assessments of caregiver burden (Caregiver Burden Scale, CBS), depressive symptoms (Geriatric Depression Scale 15-item version, GDS) and health-related quality of life (Short Form 36–Health Survey, SF-36), were performed at baseline and after 5, 12, 24, and 36 months.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-seven participants (56%) were spouses and 26 (39%) were adult children. Participation rate in assessments of outcomes at 36 months was 100% and 87% for intervention and control group in GDS and SF-36, respectively, and 69% and 61% for CBS, respectively. Missing data were primarily due to mortality. All caregivers in the intervention group (n=36) were assessed, and all received individual interventions by team staff. Twenty-three caregivers attended group sessions, and 21 completed a survey after the last session. Twenty (95%) caregivers reported increased knowledge about supporting the person with dementia, and 19 (90%) improved coping strategies. No significant differences were observed between groups in depressive symptoms or caregiver burden, yet differences in favour of the control group were seen in subscales of health-related quality of life at 24 and 36 months.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The program, combining rehabilitation for the person with dementia with caregiver support, seems feasible regarding caregivers’ participation in the intervention and study evaluation, and thus further evaluation in an adequately powered randomized controlled trial seems relevant. A future definitive trial should evaluate continuous support over a longer period adapted to the caregiver and refine assessment procedures, including conducting assessments during ongoing interventions to provide greater insights into rehabilitation and caregiver-support effects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study protocol is published online 04/11/2015 at http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN59155421.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Feasibility of a multidimensional interdisciplinary rehabilitation program for people with dementia and their informal primary caregivers – a randomized pilot trial with a caregiver focus

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Geriatric patients with multimorbidity and functional impairments represent a rapidly growing population that requires coordinated outpatient care to maintain independence and quality of life. In Germany, particularly in rural regions, outpatient care is primarily delivered by family doctors and general practitioners within a fragmented system that often lacks sufficient interdisciplinary collaboration. This fragmentation limits access to comprehensive, continuous care. Multimodal, interprofessional interventions that integrate medical, therapeutic, and psychosocial support may improve functional outcomes and reduce hospitalizations in these populations. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of a structured, multimodal, and interprofessional coordinated outpatient care model for geriatric patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This multicenter randomized controlled trial will enroll 540 geriatric patients aged 70 years and older across three regional outpatient centers (intervention centers) in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania (MV), Germany. Participants will be randomized 1:1 to receive either standard care or the Intensified Interprofessional Outpatient Therapy for Geriatric Patients (InATheGer) intervention. The intervention group will participate in a 14-week interprofessional outpatient program, comprising 20 therapy days with multimodal therapy sessions coordinated by a trained care manager (“InA-Manager”). Assessments will be conducted at baseline (before randomization), 18 weeks, and 31 weeks post-baseline. The primary outcome measure is the improvement in mobility and functional independence 18 weeks post-baseline, measured by an adapted Functional Independence Measure (FIM). Secondary outcomes include change in quality of life (EQ-5D-5 L), medication use, healthcare utilization, and costs. A qualitative process evaluation will complement the trial to explore implementation and contextual factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>If the InATheGer model demonstrates clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness, it will provide policymakers and healthcare stakeholders with evidence to inform the development and scaling of coordinated, interprofessional outpatient care for geriatric patients. Broad implementation of this model within routine geriatric outpatient care could enhance functional independence and quality of life among ageing populations while improving healthcare system efficiency.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS) registration number DRKS00036229. Prospectively registered on 08 April 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A randomized controlled trial, process and economic evaluation, comparing multimodal care intervention to standard care for older adults in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany: study protocol of the intensified interprofessional outpatient therapy for geriatric patients (InATheGer) model
Community geriatric telemedicine in Malaysia (CORTICAL©): A collaborative modified Delphi method for shared care strategies involving family medicine specialists and geriatricians
Preliminary findings on the effects of a group-based digital gaming intervention on individuals with early to moderate dementia: a pre- and post-intervention study
Association of the red blood cell distribution width-to-albumin ratio with major geriatric syndromes: a retrospective cross-sectional single-centre study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Smart wearable devices are increasingly incorporated into later-life health management, but longitudinal evidence concerning device ownership and depressive symptoms remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the within-person association between smart wearable device ownership and depressive symptoms among older adults in China, alongside concurrent psychosocial and behavioral characteristics and variation across digital and sociodemographic contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from the 2018, 2020, and 2023 waves of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey. The baseline analytical sample comprised 30,255 person-year observations from 16,752 respondents. Two-way fixed-effects models were estimated using 22,536 observations from 9,033 repeatedly observed respondents, including 902 ownership switchers. Depressive symptoms were measured using a reverse-coded nine-item CES-D score. Additional analyses examined health perception, social adaptation, leisure participation, mobile phone proficiency, sociodemographic heterogeneity, sample selection, and attrition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Smart wristband or smartwatch ownership was positively associated with the reverse-coded CES-D score within individuals (
                      <jats:italic>β =</jats:italic>
                       0.719, 95% CI [0.414, 1.024]), indicating fewer depressive symptoms during waves in which ownership was reported. The association remained positive across multiple sensitivity analyses. Ownership also covaried positively with health perception, social adaptation, and leisure participation, although their contemporaneous measurement precluded causal mediation claims. Contemporaneous analyses showed a more favorable ownership association at higher levels of self-rated mobile phone proficiency (linear interaction
                      <jats:italic>β =</jats:italic>
                       1.890,
                      <jats:italic>p <</jats:italic>
                      .001), whereas prior-proficiency analyses produced weaker evidence. Heterogeneity was statistically supported for hukou origin, but not for gender, age, or education after multiplicity adjustment.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Smart wearable device ownership was positively associated with fewer depressive symptoms within individuals, but the findings do not establish a causal effect. Digital capabilities and institutional context appear important for understanding heterogeneity in the ownership–depressive-symptom association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Smart wearable device ownership and depressive symptoms among older adults in China: a longitudinal fixed-effects analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our study aimed to analyze the latent profiles of digital health literacy among community-dwelling older adults with clinically diagnosed coronary heart disease (CHD) who can use digital devices, and to explore factors associated with different profiles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional survey was conducted among community-dwelling older adults with clinically diagnosed CHD who can use digital devices in Qingdao, from October 2024 to December 2024. Data were collected using a Demographic and Clinical questionnaire, the Older Digital Health Literacy Scale, and the Online Health Information Seeking Behavior Scale. We performed latent profile analysis to identify the latent profile of older adults with CHD. And we used chi-square and multinomial logistic regression analysis to explore associated factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 371 older coronary heart disease patients completed the questionnaire. The digital health literacy score was (39.31 ± 7.27) points. Statistical fit indices (LMR and BLRT) supported a three-class solution (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001):
                      <jats:italic>low literacy type</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 96, 26.3%),
                      <jats:italic>middle literacy type</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 188, 50.5%), and
                      <jats:italic>high literacy type</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 87, 23.2%). Place of residence, monthly household income, living arrangements, duration of coronary heart disease, frequency of using digital devices for health, and online health information seeking were significant associated with the different latent profiles (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three distinct latent profiles of digital health literacy were identified among older adults with CHD, each exhibiting significant differences in characteristics. Based on the identified profiles, tailored interventions may differ in focus: basic digital skill training for the low literacy group, guided and confidence-enhancing strategies for the middle literacy group, and advanced engagement optimization for the high literacy group. Higher levels of digital health literacy were associated with greater potential capacity for disease self-management. Notably, the findings in this study should be interpreted in light of the cross-sectional design and exclusion of non-digital-device users.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical trial number: not applicable. This study didn’t report any results of a health care intervention on human participants.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Latent profile analysis of digital health literacy among digital device-using older adults with coronary heart disease: a cross-sectional study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty syndrome is a common comorbidity in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS), significantly influencing outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Early identification of frailty and its determinants is essential for optimizing care and improving quality of life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional, observational study included 113 Polish patients qualified for TAVI between January and September 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI). Quality of life, mental health, and social support were evaluated with TASQ, HADS, and MSPSS questionnaires. Logistic regression was used to identify predictors of frailty.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty syndrome was present in 82.3% of patients. Higher frailty levels were associated with worse NYHA class, unhealthy lifestyle, and increased emotional burden. Depression and anxiety were significantly correlated with frailty, especially its psychological domain. Logistic regression revealed that NYHA class, emotional impact (TASQ), and unhealthy lifestyle were independent predictors of frailty. Social support negatively correlated with social frailty scores, suggesting a protective effect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty is highly prevalent among patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI. Comprehensive preprocedural assessment should include physical, emotional, and social factors. Targeted interventions - particularly prehabilitation and psychosocial support - may help address modifiable components of frailty in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Prevalence of frailty syndrome among patients with severe aortic stenosis qualified for TAVI
Examining polypharmacy risks and impact on clinical outcomes in older adults: insights from a cohort study

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction: This study aimed to evaluate the dose–response relationship between the Oxidative Balance Score (OBS) and a novel Gompertz law-based biological age (GOLD BioAge) and to quantify the potential mediating contributions of the Systemic Inflammation Response Index (SIRI) and uric acid to high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (UHR). Methods: This cross-sectional study included 20,930 adults aged ≥20 years (weighted mean age: 47.79 years) from seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (2001–2010 and 2015–2018). Survey-weighted regressions were used to estimate independent associations of OBS with GOLD BioAge and Accelerated GOLD BioAge. Restricted cubic spline analysis was performed to assess potential nonlinearity. Robustness was assessed through sensitivity and stratified subgroup analyses. Exploratory mediation analyses using a bootstrap resampling-based framework were performed separately for SIRI and UHR to quantify their potential mediating contributions. Results: The weighted proportion of Accelerated GOLD BioAge in the overall sample was 37.57%. The OBS was inversely and linearly associated with GOLD BioAge (P for nonlinearity = 0.723). In the fully adjusted models, each 1-point increment in OBS was associated with a 0.11-year lower GOLD BioAge (β = −0.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −0.13 to −0.10, P < 0.001) and 5% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (odds ratio [OR] = 0.95, 95% CI: 0.94 to 0.96, P < 0.001). Compared with the lowest OBS tertile (T1), the highest tertile (T3) had 51% lower odds of Accelerated GOLD BioAge (OR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.43 to 0.56, P for trend < 0.001). The inverse association was directionally consistent across examined subgroups, although its magnitude differed by sex (P for interaction < 0.001). Exploratory mediation analyses showed that SIRI and UHR accounted for 21.10% and 8.30% of the OBS–GOLD BioAge association, respectively. Conclusions: In a nationally representative sample, higher OBS was linearly associated with lower GOLD BioAge, with SIRI and UHR statistically accounting for part of this association. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that a comprehensive antioxidant-oriented dietary and lifestyle profile is associated with lower biological age, warranting further prospective investigation.</jats:p>
title: Association of the Oxidative Balance Score with GOLD BioAge: Potential Mediating Roles of SIRI and UHR among US Adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction. While residential greenspace has been linked to better cognitive function in older adults, it remains unclear whether short-term greenspace exposure during everyday mobility can provide immediate cognitive benefits. Stress may play a critical role in this process, as it reflects a mismatch between environmental demands and personal resources and may signal an increased need for restoration. Methods. This ambulatory assessment study examined the association between greenspace exposure and cognition in daily life, as well as the moderating role of stress. Over a two-week period, 123 older adults (aged 65–89 years) wore a GPS device that continuously recorded their mobility trajectories and carried a smartphone to complete repeated working memory tasks and experience sampling assessments of stressors approximately every two hours (seven times per day). Results. Multilevel models showed that, at the within-person level, greater-than-usual greenspace exposure in the past two hours was associated with higher-than-usual momentary working memory performance when stressor occurrence was reported, compared to moments when stressors were not reported. At the between-person level, individuals with higher overall greenspace exposure showed better working memory performance. Conclusions. These findings suggest that the cognitive benefits of greenspace exposure are context-dependent, emerging when stressors were recently present and when the need for restoration may be high. More broadly, our findings point to a dynamic, needs-based process in which everyday mobility through natural environments may support cognitive health among older adults.</jats:p>
title: Greenspace Exposure During Everyday Mobility and Working Memory in Older Adults: Momentary Benefits Amid Stressors

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Remote, self-administered digital assessments provide scalable approaches for monitoring cognition in older adults. Practice effects (PEs), once viewed as measurement noise, are increasingly recognized as potential markers of cognitive decline. As disease-modifying therapies for neurodegenerative conditions emerge, longitudinal digital assessments may capture subtle cognitive changes. Although the majority of PE studies have focused on memory tasks, it is critical to determine whether PEs occur in other domains. Clarifying the potential presence of PEs across multiple time points on the Food and Drug Administration–cleared Defense Automated Neurocognitive Assessment (DANA) platform remains critical for determining whether PEs can serve as a measure of cognitive decline longitudinally.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine whether PEs occur and whether demographics moderate them across quarterly self-administrations of digital cognitive tasks spanning different cognitive domains in cognitively intact older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Cognitively intact older adults from the Framingham Heart Study self-administered DANA tasks at baseline and every 3 months for 1 year (4 assessments: T1-T4). Tasks included Simple Reaction Time (SRT), Go/No-Go (GNG), and Code Substitution (CS). These tasks varied in complexity, from simple motor responding (SRT) to inhibitory control (GNG) and associative learning with working memory demands (CS). The primary outcome was Cognitive Efficiency, a derived measure of speed and accuracy, which are also recorded as secondary measures. PEs were quantified using linear mixed-effects models, and the change in mean score across time points was expressed in pooled SD units as Cohen
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A total of 717 participants completed all 4 time points (mean age 64.1, SD 9.5 years; n=469, 65.4% female participants; n=481, 67.1% college-educated). PEs were observed on all tasks, with small effects on CS (
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      =0.43) and GNG (
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      =0.32) and a below-threshold effect on SRT (
                      <jats:italic>d</jats:italic>
                      =0.16). Demographics influenced baseline performance: older age predicted lower baseline scores on all tasks, females scored lower on SRT and GNG, and higher education predicted better performance on all tasks. Age was the only demographic moderator of PEs, with smaller improvements on CS among participants aged 65 years or older (B=−0.39;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Quarterly self-administered digital cognitive assessments elicited measurable PEs across processing speed, inhibitory control, and visual scanning, with stronger effects on more complex tasks. Demographics influenced baseline performance, while age moderated PEs on the most demanding task. These findings provide baseline data against which PEs in clinical populations can be compared in future work, complementing prior evidence on other cognitive instruments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Practice Effects on Repeated Self-Administered Digital Cognitive Assessments in Cognitively Intact Older Adults from the Framingham Heart Study: Longitudinal Observational Study

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The older adult population is increasing rapidly and experiences a multitude of chronic conditions affecting quality of life. Physical activity and reduced sedentary behavior reduce adverse health conditions and help preserve functional independence and cognitive abilities, but the older adult age group has much lower levels of physical activity than recommended compared with other population demographics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study aimed to understand older adults’ motivations toward health and physical activity and the role of technology in achieving their health and physical activity goals and to explore the attitudes toward the use of generative AI in health apps.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was qualitative and based on hour-long interviews with 20 older adults living in the United States. To elicit specific design preferences, participants were presented with visual probes of AI-generated avatars. The interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, and the coding process drew on reflexive and grounded theory techniques.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults primarily wished to maintain functional independence, both physical and cognitive, prioritizing baseline maintenance rather than continuous optimization. They reported satisfaction with levels of physical activity, adjusting them to chronic conditions and injuries. They were active through everyday functions of living as well as structured exercise programs with many participants using wearable devices and smartphones to help monitor their activity. They reported being motivated by social accountability and gamification, although some found the latter condescending or anxiety-inducing. Accessibility issues were mentioned frequently, including problems with touchscreens, limited viewing, difficulty navigating interfaces with clutter, complex multitouch processes for undertaking actions, and steep learning curves. Computers were preferred for certain tasks over mobile phones due to easier viewability, keyboard access, and greater security features. Personalization was highly desired in health apps. There was a willingness to use more health technology, including generative AI, and they were willing to consider AI in both motivational and informational roles in apps as long as it was personalized. AI embodiment preferences varied widely but with an emphasis on relatability. However, there was marked skepticism toward data privacy, concerns about the loss of independence and self-efficacy, and doubts about AI’s accuracy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults are primarily motivated by sustaining functional independence, although accessibility barriers in current health apps remain. Participants were open to AI for physical activity support, but expectations varied. They viewed AI as a passive “tool,” a directive “coach,” or a relational “companion.” Considerable variation in preferences for gamification and visual design suggested that future apps require greater modularity. As skepticism over data privacy and AI accuracy remains high, greater transparency and explainability might be needed to engender trust.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Motivations, Barriers, and the Potential of AI in Physical Activity Apps for US Older Adults: Interview Study

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Health care systems increasingly offer services to citizens through online portals, which have been found to be associated with patient satisfaction and better management of health concerns. Few studies have compared self-reported use with objectively documented portal use, especially among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine differences between documented and self-reported health portal use, and their associations with background variables and digital health literacy (DHL) among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted among 600 participants aged 60 years and older, who were sampled from a registry of members of a national health maintenance organization (HMO). The participants reported their use of the HMO’s portal, their DHL, and demographic and background variables. Participants’ use of the portal was retrospectively retrieved from the HMO’s administrative database.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A large gap between self-reported use and documented use of the health portal was found: for example, while only 8.1% (46/566) reported not using the portal, the HMO’s records indicated that 62% (372/600) did not make use of the portal. However, a positive correlation was found between self-reported use and documented use (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). Significant positive associations were found between administrative and physician-related online services, both reported use (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.41;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) and documented use (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.56;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001). A multivariate analysis, where documented use was the dependent variable, explained 12.5% of the variance. Experience with computers (β=0.13;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02) and ethnicity (β=−0.22;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) were significantly associated with documented use. DHL, though significantly associated with documented use at the bivariate level (
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.09;
                      <jats:italic>P=</jats:italic>
                      .04), was not significantly associated with documented use in this analysis (β=0.02;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.97).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that users tend to overestimate their health portal use. Interpretations vary from measurement issues, such as social desirability bias regarding digital functioning or the perception that assisted use also constitutes usage, to signaling their identity as engaged digital health consumers. Future studies on digital health use should also include measures of electronically documented use and not only self-reported use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Gaps Between Self-Reported and Documented Use of a Health Care Service Portal Among Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Survey and Retrospective Electronic Data Study

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early population-based screening for Alzheimer’s disease remains limited by the scalability and accessibility of conventional biomarker testing. We tested whether passive naturalistic driving changes predict progression from cognitively normal status to sustained mild cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Season-adjusted monthly driving data from 298 older adults, including 25 progressors, were summarized into within-person trajectory features capturing drift and instability in cornering and destination diversity relative to a six-month baseline. A GEE logistic regression was evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation with a paired-consecutive flagging rule. Landmark survival analyses at 12 and 24 months assessed prognostic value. Five held-out clinical subgroups (n = 82 evaluable), plasma pTau217, MoCA trajectories, and depression scores provided independent post hoc validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model detected 19/25 progressors (AUC=0.752, 95%CI: 0.627–0.863; 76% sensitivity; 75% specificity) with an 18-month median lead time before sustained CDR conversion. Adding static baseline driving features reduced discrimination (AUC=0.702), supporting that within-person driving change, not absolute level, carries a predictive signal. Driving markers stratified risk at 12 months (HR = 6.02, 95%CI: 2.35–15.41) and 24 months (HR = 13.38, 95%CI: 3.03–59.04). Signals converged or were directionally consistent with higher pTau217 among detected progressors and clinically ambiguous single-endpoint cases, whereas flagged stable participants showed MoCA decline without pTau217 enrichment. Depressive symptoms did not explain the driving signal (Spearman rho=0.05, p=0.53). The sustained conversion rate (12.3/1,000 person-years) matched epidemiological expectations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Scalable driving-trajectory features can detect preclinical functional decline with clinically meaningful lead time, without demographic, genetic, or cognitive data, and may serve as an objective neurobehavioral screening tool.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Naturalistic Driving Engineered Trajectories Forecast Future Cognitive Decline

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Family caregivers of individuals with Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) work with healthcare providers to ensure effective care coordination on behalf of the care recipient. However, challenges within the caregiver-healthcare provider relationship are common and may contribute to poor caregiver health outcomes. This study examined the impact of perceived quality of the relationship between family caregivers and healthcare providers and the caregivers’ daily mental health symptom burden (depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 228 family caregivers who lived with and provided unpaid care to a family member with dementia. Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) were developed to assess whether the caregiver-provider relationship was associated with caregiver daily depressive symptoms, daily anxiety, and daily stress.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 228 caregivers, 82% were female, 84% were spouses or partners of the care recipient, and 9% of caregivers were classified as living in poverty. Caregivers who rated their providers’ affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) more positively reported lower daily depressive symptoms (β= -0.06, p = .001) and anxiety symptoms (β= -0.07, p &lt; .001). The caregiver-provider relationship was not associated with daily stress experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings from the study suggest that healthcare provider affect (perceptions of being valued, respected, and emotionally supported) may be a protective factor, especially against depressive symptoms and anxiety, and offer an avenue for future interventions. Integrating caregiver-provider relationship-informed practices into routine dementia care may help foster emotionally responsive, person- and family-centered care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Caregiver-provider relationship quality and health outcomes in family caregivers of people living with dementia

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Psychological richness, a dimension of well-being characterized by novelty, complexity, and perspective change, is theoretically grounded in varied and unusual experiences. This study examined whether daily activity diversity was associated with psychological richness in two cohorts of midlife and older adults from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Daily reports were drawn from two cohorts of the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) study: MIDUS 2 (M2; N = 1,834) and the MIDUS Refresher (MR; N = 730). Daily activity diversity was quantified with Shannon entropy, capturing both the breadth and evenness of participants' daily activities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower activity diversity was associated with higher psychological richness in both cohorts (M2: β = −0.07, p &lt;.001; MR: β = −0.06, p = .009). After adjustment for age, sex, education, race, and chronic health conditions, associations were inverse in both cohorts but statistically significant only in M2 (M2: β = −0.07, p &lt;.001; MR: β = −0.04, p = .068).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that broader activity repertoires do not necessarily correspond to greater psychological richness and that psychologically rich lives may coexist with relatively narrow patterns of daily engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Activity diversity and psychological richness across midlife and older adulthood

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated whether cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) in young adulthood is associated with depressive symptoms several decades later and if later-life physical activity and self-rated health mediate this association.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample comprised 690 Swedish men completing a CRF test at age 18 and self-reported depressive symptoms around age 61. Unadjusted and adjusted logistic and linear regression models and Bayesian mediation analyses were estimated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Medium and high CRF at age 18, compared with low CRF, were associated with lower odds of clinically significant depressive symptoms in late adulthood. The odds ratios of clinically significant depressive symptoms were 0.329 (95% CI [0.157, 0.687]) for men with medium and 0.383 (95% CI [0.157, 0.939]) for men with high CRF compared with those with low CRF. No credible mediated associations were observed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that promoting fitness early in life may represent a useful preventive strategy for mental health resilience across the life course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness in Young Adulthood and Depressive Symptoms Later in Life Among Swedish Men

                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Turnover among non-nursing staff such as housekeeping, dietary, laundry, and maintenance workers is a growing concern in nursing homes. To our knowledge, only Iowa collects systematic data on turnover for these roles. Because these workers are essential to daily services for older adults, understanding their turnover trends is critical.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used turnover data from all Iowa nursing homes from 2009 to 2022 to summarize annual turnover rates and examine trends over time, stratified by profit status, rurality, and overall quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample included 421 nursing homes with 5,130 facility-year observations. Turnover increased over time for all staff types; in 2022, turnover rates were 88.1% for housekeeping, 87.8% for dietary, 53.9% for laundry, and 43.6% for maintenance. Turnover was higher in for-profit, urban, and lower-quality facilities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Non-nursing staff turnover in nursing homes is extremely high. Broader data collection is needed to evaluate its impact on quality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Turnover of Housekeeping, Dietary, Laundry, and Maintenance Staff in Nursing Homes

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Financial fraud and exploitation (FFE) are associated with billions of dollars lost annually and have significant adverse effects on older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given the challenges and complexities of FFE identification and response, this study aimed to identify domains associated with elder FFE risk from a multidisciplinary perspective.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This qualitative study interviewed experts within the field through six qualitative focus groups conducted in 2024. A thematic analysis approach was used to identify themes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five domains were identified encompassing intersecting factors associated with elder FFE: cognitive health, individual behaviors, social health, financial well-being, and health and environment considerations. These findings demonstrate nuanced FFE risk considerations and the need to approach assessment models from a multidisciplinary, accessible perspective to enhance financial empowerment in older adulthood. Findings will be used to inform development of a financial tool to assess potential risk for FFE among older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Grounded in Experience: Designing the Financial Empowerment Scale Through Community Dialogues

records.abstract: <jats:p>Hypertension is highly prevalent among adults aged 45 years and older in India, yet limited evidence exists on the combined associations of waist circumference (WC) and body mass index (BMI) with hypertension. This study examined their independent and joint associations with hypertension using Wave 1 (2017–18) of the Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (LASI) among 59,658 adults aged 45 years and older. Hypertension was defined as measured blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations across combined WC–BMI categories. Overall hypertension prevalence was 31.3%. Individuals with normal BMI but large WC had higher odds of hypertension (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 1.37; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.19–1.58). Obese individuals with large WC had the highest odds (AOR = 1.77; 95% CI: 1.45–2.17). Both central and general obesity were independently associated with hypertension. Routine WC assessment alongside BMI may improve identification of high-risk individuals in India’s middle-aged and older population.</jats:p>
title: Beyond BMI: The Role of Abdominal Obesity in Hypertension Risk Among Adults Aged 45 Years and Older in India

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cancer patients experience suboptimal care in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs). Medicare’s Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) incentivized SNFs to admit complex patients, potentially promoting admissions without appropriate changes in care delivery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate changes in SNF admissions, rehabilitation therapy volume, and chemotherapy/radiation around admission or discharge, following PDPM and COVID-19.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adjusted interrupted time series examining 1,125,782 hospital stays from metastatic cancer patients, using 100% Traditional Medicare claims (2018–2021).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PDPM was associated with increased SNF admissions (0.47 pp/month; 95% CI: [0.17, 0.76]) and an immediate reduction in therapy volume (−24.95 minutes per day, 95% CI: [−26.40, −23.48]). Chemotherapy use remained low, but increased by 21% at PDPM implementation, without subsequent slope change (RR: 1.21; 95% CI: [1.01, 1.46]); radiation was unchanged. COVID-19 reversed admission gains. SNF admissions for metastatic cancer patients increased without sustained changes in cancer-relevant care delivery, warranting investigation of health outcomes and outcome-driven policy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Incentives for Access: Changes in Admissions and Care Delivery for Metastatic Cancer Patients in Medicare Skilled Nursing Facilities, After the Patient-Driven Payment Model

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While WHO ICOPE screening is routine, the association between multi-domain intrinsic capacity (IC) decline and falls remains understudied in community-based gerontology practice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study analysed 775 rural older adults (mean age 79.4) with ≥1 IC abnormality using multivariable logistic regression and dose–response analysis to evaluate fall risk.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>

                      <jats:sub>trend</jats:sub>
                      <.001). Clusters involving depression with mobility or vision identified the highest-risk subgroups (34–36% fall rate).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An IC impairment count of ≥3, or specific clusters (nutrition, mobility, depression), provides practical triage criteria for community-based fall-prevention. These findings facilitate person-centred risk stratification and resource allocation within integrated care systems for super-aging societies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Multi-Domain Intrinsic Capacity Decline and Fall History Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Rural Taiwan: Implications for ICOPE-Based Community Screening

<jats:p>
                    The Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) is a brief screening tool that assesses the presence and severity of insomnia symptoms. Although widely validated, its psychometric properties remain understudied in older adults, a population at increased risk for insomnia due to age-related changes in sleep architecture and quality. This study assessed the concurrent and factorial validity of the ISI among community-dwelling older adults (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                     = 250) who completed the ISI and measures of comorbid symptoms: Brief Geriatric Suicide Ideation Scale, Michigan Alcohol Screening Test-Geriatric Version, Geriatric Depression Scale-15, and Geriatric Anxiety Scale. Bivariate correlations supported concurrent validity, with insomnia positively associated with anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation, and alcohol misuse. Anxiety was the strongest correlate and the only unique predictor of ISI scores in multivariate analyses. Exploratory factor analysis revealed a one-factor solution. Findings support the concurrent validity and factor structure of the ISI and highlight comorbidity with other mental health symptoms among older adults.
                  </jats:p>
title: Comorbid Psychopathology of Insomnia: A Validity Study of the Insomnia Severity Index Among Older Adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Summer Training and Research Program (Hopkins USTAR) was a 2-year program funded by the National Institute on Aging R25 Advancing Diversity in Aging Research through Undergraduate Education. Hopkins USTAR was designed to provide undergraduate students primarily from underrepresented backgrounds in biomedical and behavioral science with interdisciplinary research training in aging and health disparities research. From 2023 to 2025, a total of 15 undergraduate students participated in faculty-mentored research projects, professional development, research education, and national research conferences. Program evaluation methods included pre- and post-program surveys and interviews. Results suggest that the Hopkins USTAR program significantly increased aspects of participants’ research self-efficacy and strengthened perceived science identity. Despite the early termination of Hopkins USTAR, the program's short-term outcomes indicate modest success in fostering positive feelings about science and preparing participants for graduate school. Continued follow-up to assess long-term program outcomes will be important to measure impact.</jats:p>
title: Mentoring Undergraduates in Aging and Disparities Research: Hopkins USTAR

records.abstract: <jats:p>The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults’ entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults’ sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a “conditional crossing” mechanism for older adults’ acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.</jats:p>
title: Crossing the Digital Divide: Understanding Older Adults’ Technology Acceptance of Generative Artificial Intelligence: A Qualitative Study

records.abstract: <jats:p>Dementia prevention is receiving increasing attention considering the surge in number of dementia incidence worldwide. Although there are modifiable risk factors, the public remains largely unaware of dementia prevention. Many individuals turn to online platforms such as YouTube for health-related information, where content can shape beliefs, attitudes, and decision-making. However, little is known about how people interpret and discuss dementia prevention in these digital spaces. This study aimed to explore how dementia prevention is perceived by the public, as reflected in user generated comments posted on YouTube videos related to dementia prevention. A qualitative thematic analysis was conducted by examining comments from YouTube videos identified through Google Advanced Search. Twenty-six videos were selected based on predefined criteria, and comments were extracted and cleaned prior to analysis. Engagement metrics, including views, likes, and replies, were also examined to understand how users interacted with the content. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-step thematic approach. A total of 7314 comments were retrieved from 26 videos. Following data cleaning and removal of ineligible comments, 2034 comments were included for final analysis. Thematic analysis revealed three themes: (i) fear and perceived vulnerability to dementia; (ii) perceptions of dementia risk factors; and (iii) trust and credibility of dementia prevention information. These themes revealed fear, modifiable vs non-modifiable risk factors, and both public reliance on and distrust of scientific evidence. YouTube provides an important platform for public discussion about dementia prevention. Although it offers opportunities to increase awareness, viewer comments reflected inconsistent understandings and conflicting beliefs about dementia prevention, highlighting the need for clear, evidence-based communication to improve public understanding.</jats:p>
title: Perceptions of Dementia Prevention on YouTube: A Thematic Analysis of Viewer Comments

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Age-related changes in gut microbiota composition have been implicated in brain aging and cognitive decline, acting through the gut-brain axis on amyloid accumulation, tau pathology, synapse damage, and glial activation. Live microbial approaches such as probiotics, prebiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation address this mechanism, but they still suffer from low efficacy and unknown safety issues. We tested whether abdominal ultrasound, an approach that does not involve microbes, can alleviate age-related neurodegeneration in the senescence-accelerated mouse strain SAMP8. We treated 6-month-old male SAMP8 mice for 1 month. We then assessed behavior, neuropathology, and synaptic proteins, and quantified four pre-specified fecal bacterial taxa. Ultrasound preserved neuronal survival in the hippocampal CA3, decreased amyloid-β load in the cortex and CA3, decreased tau hyperphosphorylation in all three regions, reduced Iba-1 and GFAP immunoreactive areas, and increased synaptophysin and cortical PSD-95. Neuronal survival in the cortex and CA1 did not differ significantly from sham-treated SAMP8 mice. In the gut microbiota, ultrasound significantly reduced the enriched taxon Tyzzerella, whereas the changes in Lactobacillus, Akkermansia and Atopobiaceae were large in magnitude but not statistically significant. In an exploratory analysis, four of 64 microbiota–neuropathology associations survived correction for multiple testing. Neither object recognition memory nor spatial memory differed significantly between treated and sham-treated SAMP8 mice. Abdominal ultrasound applied to the periphery therefore reduced age-associated neuropathology in the brain, accompanied by changes in specific gut microbial taxa whose causal contribution remains untested.</jats:p>
title: Abdominal ultrasound mitigates neurodegenerative pathology and alters specific gut microbial taxa in senescence-accelerated mice

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although cycling offers numerous health benefits, age-related functional decline can increase the risk of accidents. Identifying balance components linked to outdoor cycling competence could inform targeted assessment and training. We aimed to exploratorily investigate the association between outdoor cycling competence and static, dynamic, and reactive balance control in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this exploratory cross-sectional analysis of baseline data from a two-center randomized controlled trial, 116 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years with ≥ 3 errors on a standardized outdoor cycling course completed a balance test battery: Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB), including gait speed, Modified Balance Error Scoring System (MBESS) and Four Square Step Test (FSST). Cycling-specific trunk balance was assessed with the Perturbation Stationary Bicycle Robotics (PerStBiRo) system, which delivers unannounced angular-tilt perturbations during stationary cycling. We derived mediolateral (ML) trunk sway during unperturbed cycling (UPC) and trunk time-to-peak angle (s) and trunk sway (°) during perturbed cycling (PC). Spearman correlations and multivariable models adjusted for age, sex and country were used to examine associations with the number of errors in the standardized outdoor cycling course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants (mean age 74.0 ± 5.4 years; 53% women) made 13.1 ± 8.0 errors on the outdoor cycling course. In bivariate analyses, more outdoor cycling errors were weakly associated with more total errors on the MBESS (r
                      <jats:sub>s</jats:sub>
                      = 0.213,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.022), slower gait speed (r
                      <jats:sub>s</jats:sub>
                      = -0.203,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.029), greater ML trunk sway during UPC (r
                      <jats:sub>s</jats:sub>
                      = 0.246,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.009), shorter trunk time-to-peak angle (r
                      <jats:sub>s</jats:sub>
                      = -0.289,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002) and lower trunk sway in PC (r
                      <jats:sub>s</jats:sub>
                      = -0.295,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.002). In multivariable analyses, longer FSST time (B = 1.28 [95% CI 0.39, 2.17],
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005) and greater trunk sway during UPC (B = 2.68 [0.60, 4.77],
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.012) were independently associated with more cycling errors.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study shows weak associations between outdoor cycling competence and dynamic balance control during both UPC and FSST. Low trunk sway during UPC on the PerStBiRo is weakly associated with better outdoor cycling competence. These findings could be further evaluated in future studies aiming to improve outdoor cycling competence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      This is a retrospective analysis of BiPerAge study data registered at clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06453473 (initial submission: 11/06/2024), link:
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06453473" ext-link-type="uri">https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06453473</jats:ext-link>
                      .

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty is associated with hip fractures in older adults. However, frailty is a dynamic process, longitudinal trajectories may provide complementary descriptive insights. The exploratory association between frailty trajectories and hip fracture risk remains uncertain, particularly in older Chinese adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed longitudinal data from 3,868 community-dwelling Chinese adults aged ≥ 65 years in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS). Frailty was assessed using the CHARLS modified frailty index (CMFI). Latent class mixed models were used descriptively to characterize frailty trajectories. The primary risk analysis used baseline CMFI, measured before follow-up, to evaluate associations with incident hip fractures using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models. Restricted cubic splines were employed to explore nonlinear relationships. Associations between frailty trajectory class and hip fracture were also examined as exploratory analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>During a median follow-up of 7.2 years, 225 incident hip fractures occurred. Two frailty trajectory patterns were identified descriptively: slow-rising and fast-rising. The primary finding was that each 0.1-unit increase in baseline CMFI was associated with a 32% higher risk (HR = 1.32, 95% CI: 1.19–1.46), and this association persisted after accounting for the competing risk of death (SHR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.07–1.31). A non-linear relationship was observed, suggesting a possible attenuation of the association at higher frailty levels. The associations were generally consistent across the subgroups. In exploratory analyses, the fast-rising trajectory was associated with a higher hazard of hip fracture (HR = 2.39, 95% CI: 1.77–3.23; SHR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.49–2.84).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher baseline frailty was independently associated with a higher risk of hip fracture. The fast-rising trajectory showed a higher hazard in descriptive analyses but requires time-varying validation. Dynamic frailty monitoring may aid risk stratification, pending future time-varying and external validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Frailty trajectories and hip fracture risk in older Chinese adults: a prospective cohort study with competing risk analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Major lower extremity amputation for diabetic foot complications is associated with substantial mortality, particularly in older adults. We evaluated whether routinely available preoperative laboratory parameters provide prognostic information for 24-month mortality and developed an exploratory laboratory-based risk score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This retrospective cohort study included 72 patients aged ≥ 65 years who underwent transtibial or transfemoral amputation for diabetic foot complications between January 2021 and June 2023 at a tertiary referral center. Vital status was ascertained through July 31, 2025. Associations with 24-month all-cause mortality were evaluated using Cox proportional hazards regression. A 3-point score was derived from laboratory predictors using receiver operating characteristic analysis and Youden-index-based thresholds. Model discrimination and calibration were assessed, and bootstrap optimism correction was applied to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. The proposed score was additionally compared with the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), and Hemoglobin–Albumin–Lymphocyte–Platelet (HALP) score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Thirty-nine patients (54.2%) died within 24 months. Kaplan–Meier-estimated 24-month survival was 45.8% (95% CI 34.1–56.8%). In multivariable Cox analysis, higher hemoglobin (adjusted HR 1.302, 95% CI 1.041–1.628;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.021), lower platelet count (adjusted HR 0.9966, 95% CI 0.9939–0.9994;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.017), and lower albumin (adjusted HR 0.868, 95% CI 0.813–0.927;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) were independently associated with mortality. One point was assigned for hemoglobin > 10.3 g/dL, platelet count < 342.5 × 10⁹/L, and albumin < 28.5 g/L. Patients with scores ≥ 2 had substantially lower 24-month survival than those with scores 0–1 (8.0% vs. 66.0%; log-rank
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). The score had an AUC of 0.798 for 24-month mortality. The underlying Cox model had an optimism-corrected C-index of 0.712. The score showed numerically higher discrimination than GNRI (AUC 0.739) and PNI (0.735), and higher discrimination than HALP (0.590).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A simple score based on albumin, hemoglobin, and platelet count showed promising prognostic discrimination for 24-month mortality after major amputation in this geriatric diabetic foot cohort. Quantitative ischemia severity and standardized neuropathy and frailty assessments were unavailable, and the score was derived and evaluated in the same derivation cohort, while bootstrap optimism correction was limited to the fixed three-biomarker Cox model. It should therefore be regarded as exploratory, should not replace comprehensive clinical and vascular assessment, and requires external validation before clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development of an exploratory preoperative laboratory-based score for 24-month mortality after major lower extremity amputation in geriatric diabetic foot patients
