<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malnutrition is highly prevalent in geriatric trauma patients and is associated with impaired recovery, complications, and reduced likelihood of returning home. Nonetheless, the impact of a targeted protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay on patient outcome and rehabilitation remains to be investigated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This single-center randomized controlled study enrolled patients ≥ 70 years with fragility fractures admitted to a Level I trauma center. Nutritional status was assessed using the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 and Mini Nutritional Assessment. Patients screened positive in ≥ 1 tool were classified as being at nutritional risk and randomized to a protein-enriched diet (Group A) or standard diet (Group B); patients with negative screening served as observational reference group without nutritional risk (Group C). The intervention targeted 1.5–2.0 g/kg/day protein. Primary outcomes were in-hospital medical complications, surgical site infections and functional mobility at discharge. Secondary outcomes included length of stay, discharge destination, and in-hospital mortality. Multinomial logistic regression assessed independent associations with discharge destination.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Of the 218 patients (mean age 81.8 ± 6.9 years; 72.0% female), 100 (45.9%) screened positive for being at nutritional risk and were randomized to intervention (A,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 46) or control (B,
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 54), while 118 (54.1%) patients without nutritional risk served as reference group (C). Patients at nutritional risk showed higher comorbidity burdens, higher ASA classes, and greater frailty than group C. Medical complications occurred in 45.0% of patients, with no significant differences between groups. Serum albumin decreased and CRP increased during hospitalization, without differences among the groups. Patients in reference group C were more often independently mobile and discharged home, whereas all patients at nutritional risk more frequently required institutional care. In multivariable analysis, a higher age-adjusted CCI was independently associated with discharge destination, whereas no independent effect of the nutritional intervention was observed.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this geriatric trauma cohort, being at nutritional risk was closely linked to frailty and multimorbidity. A protein-enriched diet during the acute hospital stay did not translate into measurable short-term benefits regarding complications, functional mobility, length of stay or discharge destination. Nutritional risk should therefore be considered within the broader context of overall vulnerability, and nutritional care may need to be embedded in comprehensive longitudinal rehabilitation strategies extending beyond the acute in-hospital phase.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov on 12 May 2026 (NCT07582575).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Impact of malnutrition and protein-enriched oral nutrition on early recovery after fragility fractures in older adults: the NuTra trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity is common in older adults and has been associated with adverse cognitive outcomes. However, findings remain heterogeneous because of differences in multimorbidity definitions, cognitive measures, and study designs. This review aimed to synthesize evidence on the association between multimorbidity and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and gray literature sources were searched up to August 2026. Observational studies examining multimorbidity, defined as ≥ 2 chronic conditions, and cognitive outcomes in adults aged ≥ 60 years were included. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute checklists, and findings were synthesized narratively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seventeen studies met the eligibility criteria. Overall, greater multimorbidity burden was generally associated with poorer cognitive outcomes, while several specific multimorbidity patterns, particularly cardiometabolic and cardiovascular patterns, were associated with cognitive impairment, cognitive decline, or dementia. However, some studies reported null or domain-specific associations. Considerable heterogeneity was observed across multimorbidity definitions, cognitive assessments, study designs, populations, and confounding adjustment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multimorbidity may be associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in older adults, but the strength and consistency of the evidence vary across studies. Interpretation is limited by methodological heterogeneity, potential risk of bias, and the observational nature of the evidence. More standardized prospective studies are needed to clarify these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: From chronic disease burden to cognitive decline: a systematic review of multimorbidity in older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As one of the newest disease-modifying therapies for early Alzheimer’s disease, lecanemab has attracted widespread research interest in various clinical settings around the world. However, there is currently insufficient understanding of patients’ and family caregivers’ real-world treatment experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed an exploratory qualitative research design and conducted semi-structured in-depth interviews with family caregivers of patients with early AD who are currently receiving lecanemab treatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three themes emerged: (1) Experiences and Attitudes Toward Lecanemab Treatment; (2) The Multiple Practical Challenges of Treatment Costs, Informed Decision-Making, and Efficacy Assessment; (3) Strategies for Future Improvements.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Given the current state of healthcare in China, families of Alzheimer’s patients still have high hopes for lecanemab treatment. Although some patients report that it has slowed the rate of cognitive decline, factors such as high costs and significant side effects make treatment decisions extremely complex.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Impact</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings provide valuable real-world insights into the use of Lecanemab in Chinese Alzheimer’s patients, thereby informing and improving the design of future clinical studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Reporting method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adhered to the COREQ guideline.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Public contributions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>No paper or public contribution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Navigating a new era of disease-modifying therapy: experiences, treatment preferences, and unmet expectations of family caregivers of Alzheimer’s patients receiving lecanemab in China

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although greater life enjoyment is associated with a lower risk of frailty, little is known about the association between sources of life enjoyment and frailty. This study investigated the associations between the variety and types of sources of enjoyment in life (“enjoyment sources”) and frailty among community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses were conducted using data from a community-based cohort study in Japan. In 2020, questionnaires were mailed to 4,996 randomly selected adults aged ≥65 years, and 2,764 responded. Follow-up questionnaires were sent to 1,635 consenting participants in 2023, with 904 responses obtained. Frailty was assessed using a 5-item self-report questionnaire at baseline and follow-up. Enjoyment sources were assessed through yes/no and open-ended questions at baseline and categorized using content analysis. The number of identified categories was counted, and participants were classified into no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional analysis included 2,361 participants, and the prevalence of frailty was 26.6%, 16.7%, and 11.3% in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. Cross-sectional analyses showed that a greater variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of both prefrailty and frailty. In the 3-year longitudinal analysis, 688 participants were included. Among them, incident frailty occurred in 20.2%, 11.1%, and 10.0% of participants in the no-source, single-source, and multiple-source groups, respectively. The variety of enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of incident frailty in both crude and basic adjusted models. The odds ratios for the single-source and multiple-source groups were similar. Exploratory analysis of the 10 most frequently reported enjoyment sources showed that books, sports, friends, foods, and singing/playing musical instruments showed inverse trends with frailty, whereas media consumption showed a positive trend with frailty in unadjusted cross-sectional trend tests.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Having one or more enjoyment sources was associated with lower odds of frailty among community-dwelling older adults in both cross-sectional and 3-year longitudinal analyses. The exploratory analysis also suggested that the associations between specific types of enjoyment sources and frailty may differ.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Sources of enjoyment in life and frailty among community-dwelling older adults: cross-sectional and longitudinal associations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The decline in musculoskeletal function with aging is a key contributor to mobility impairments and loss of independence. While sarcopenia and dynapenia are well described, recent evidence highlights muscle power as a more sensitive indicator of functional deterioration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to compare age-associated differences in muscle mass, force, and lower-limb muscle power in older adults over different assessment methods, while accounting for sex-related differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three hundred nineteen community-dwelling adults aged 60–97 years were assessed for muscle mass (DXA-derived lean mass, appendicular skeletal muscle mass index), muscle force (handgrip force, knee extension maximal isometric contraction), muscle moments and angular velocity (isokinetic dynamometry), and lower-limb muscle power (isokinetic testing and sit-to-stand power). Associations with age and sex were examined using regression models and ANOVA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Lower-limb muscle power showed a stronger negative association with age than muscle force or mass (β = − 0.433 vs. − 0.303 and − 0.119, respectively;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). However, the present study could not determine whether muscle power begins to decline earlier than muscle force or mass. For several variables, age associations were stronger in males than in females, most consistently for lower-limb power, although these interactions were not systematically reproduced in age-stratified analyses. The strongest negative age associations were observed between 71 and 80 years, whereas fewer significant associations (only for handgrip) were observed after age 80.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower-limb muscle power appeared more sensitive to age-associated differences than muscle force or mass, supporting its role as a key biomarker of neuromuscular aging. This study also highlights that sex may contribute to variability in age-associated patterns of muscle power, raising questions about the universality of its definition that warrant further confirmation. These findings emphasize the clinical importance of including power assessments in strategies to preserve independence in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05343286,
                      <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286" ext-link-type="uri">https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT05343286</jats:ext-link>
                      .
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Age-associated differences in lower-extremity muscle mass, force, and power in older adults: a cross-sectional analysis of sex differences

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance and agreement of calculated serum osmolarity for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients, using clinical impression of dehydration as the reference standard, and to examine glucose levels across concordant and discordant classification groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design and setting</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective, observational study was conducted in a geriatric acute care unit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study included 455 older hospitalized patients with a mean age of 82.2 ± 6.8 years and 70% were female.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Measurements</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinical impression of dehydration (dehydration vs. no dehydration [normal hydration + hyperhydration]) was judged and recorded by the attending physician within 24 h of admission. Calculated serum osmolarity was derived from routine laboratory values and classified as high (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) or normal (< 295 mOsmol/l). Diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, accuracy) and agreement (Cohen’s κ) were calculated. Glucose was compared between concordant/discordant groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Clinically, 23% of patients were classified as dehydrated. High calculated osmolarity occurred in 38%. Using the ≥ 295 mOsmol/l cut-off, sensitivity was 48.6% and specificity 65.1%; positive and negative predictive values were 29.7% and 80.7%, respectively, and accuracy was 61.3%. Agreement beyond chance was poor (κ = 0.112). Mean glucose was higher in osmolarity-positive groups, including false positives (all
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001 for planned pairwise comparisons).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In older hospitalized patients, calculated serum osmolarity (≥ 295 mOsmol/l) showed limited agreement with clinical dehydration assessment with frequent osmolarity-positive classifications in clinically non-dehydrated patients. These findings support cautious clinical interpretation of calculated osmolarity in acute care, particularly when glucose is elevated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Diagnostic performance of calculated serum osmolarity versus clinical impression for identifying dehydration in older hospitalized patients

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Dysphagia is a critical geriatric syndrome associated with an increased risk of aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, and mortality in older adults. The aim of this study was to evaluate the associations between Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) parameters and dysphagia risk (Eating Assessment Tool-10 (EAT-10) ≥ 3) in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This cross-sectional study included 468 community-dwelling older adults presenting to a geriatric outpatient clinic. Participants with severe cognitive impairment, Parkinson’s disease, those residing in a nursing home, and those with an acute medical condition were excluded from the study. Dysphagia risk was assessed using the EAT-10; probable sarcopenia was defined according to the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2019 (EWGSOP2) criteria; depressive symptoms were evaluated with the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15); and nutritional status was assessed using the Mini Nutritional Assessment–Short Form (MNA-SF). Independent risk factors were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      In the final multivariate regression model, the presence of probable sarcopenia (OR = 2.654, 95% CI: 1.184–5.947,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.018) and higher GDS-15 scores (OR = 1.155, 95% CI: 1.063–1.255,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001) were independently and significantly associated with dysphagia risk. In contrast, a one-point increase in the MNA-SF score (indicating better nutritional status), when treated as a continuous variable, was an independent protective factor against dysphagia risk (OR = 0.684, 95% CI: 0.521–0.897,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.006).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In community-dwelling older adults, probable sarcopenia and depressive symptoms significantly increase the dysphagia risk, whereas good nutritional status plays a protective role. Prior to the development of dysphagia and its associated complications, optimizing muscle strength, mood, and nutritional status in outpatient settings is of importance for maintaining swallowing safety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Probable sarcopenia, depressive symptoms, and nutritional status as independent predictors of dysphagia risk in community-dwelling older adults

records.abstract: <jats:p>Background:Osteoporosis and fragility fractures are major causes of disability, loss of independence, institutionalization, and mortality in the oldest old. Despite their exceptionally high fracture risk, adults aged ≥80 years remain underrepresented in randomized controlled trials. Diagnosis and treatment are complicated by the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, sarcopenia, frailty, multimorbidity, cognitive and functional impairment, and competing mortality. Summary: This narrative review discusses the diagnosis, fracture-risk assessment, non-pharmacological management, and pharmacological treatment of osteoporosis in the oldest old. Bone mineral density (BMD) remains central to osteoporosis diagnosis but incompletely characterizes fracture risk at advanced age. Previous and particularly recent fractures, prevalent vertebral fractures, falls, physical performance, nutritional status, and frailty provide complementary information. Interpretation of the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool FRAX® requires particular consideration in the oldest old because competing mortality may cause 10-year fracture probabilities to plateau or decline despite increasing age-specific fracture incidence; FRAXplus® incorporates additional risk modifiers, including falls and the number and recency of previous fractures. Non-pharmacological interventions addressing nutrition, muscle function, balance, and falls complement bone-directed pharmacotherapy. Available evidence does not indicate that chronological age itself attenuates the efficacy of osteoporosis pharmacotherapy, although direct randomized fracture-endpoint evidence in adults aged ≥80 years remains limited. Risedronate and, historically, strontium ranelate provide some of the clearest fracture data specifically in this age group, whereas evidence for most other therapies derives from older-subgroup analyses, skeletal efficacy studies, observational data, or extrapolation from pivotal trials. At advanced age, renal function, cognition, mobility, adherence, caregiver support, and continuity of care increasingly influence the translation of efficacy into clinical effectiveness. Key Messages: Fracture risk in the oldest old reflects the interaction of skeletal fragility with falls, frailty, sarcopenia, and functional reserve. Available evidence supports preservation of pharmacological antifracture efficacy with advancing age, but direct evidence in octogenarians and particularly nonagenarians remains scarce. Treatment feasibility and continuity of care become increasingly relevant at advanced age. Greater representation of the oldest old in clinical trials is needed, with particular attention to fracture outcomes, treatment sequencing, time to benefit, and outcomes relevant to independence and quality of life.</jats:p>
title: Osteoporosis in the Oldest Old - From Diagnosis to Treatment: A Narrative Review

records.abstract: <jats:p>Introduction Diabetic retinopathy, which occurs during extended periods of chronic hyperglycemia, is one of the main causes of vision loss. The receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) plays a central role in inflammatory and angiogenic signaling, both of which contribute to the pathogenesis of diabetic retinopathy, but its therapeutic targeting in ocular disease has been insufficiently explored. Methods We evaluated topical RAGE229, a small-molecule RAGE inhibitor, and an intravitreally administered anti-RAGE antibody in a streptozotocin-induced diabetic rat model. At day 84, treatment effects were assessed using masked fundoscopic scoring, RT-qPCR, immunohistochemistry, and histological morphometry. Treated eyes were evaluated against both route-matched diabetic vehicle-control groups and paired contralateral vehicle-treated eyes. Results Both interventions reduced fundoscopic pathology and retinal Vegfa and Nfkb1 expression, whereas Ager showed only a non-significant downward trend. NF-κB p65 immunoreactivity was reduced by both treatments, while a significant reduction in VEGF-A immunoreactivity was detected only in the paired anti-RAGE antibody analysis. Morphometric analysis indicated attenuation of diabetes-associated retinal thinning with both interventions. Neither intervention altered systemic glycemic control. Although both interventions demonstrated similar overall anatomical protection, anti-RAGE antibody treatment showed more consistent effects across protein-level and structural endpoints. Conclusion These findings provide proof-of-concept evidence that local RAGE-targeted treatment may attenuate vascular, molecular, and structural manifestations of early experimental diabetic retinopathy without detectable changes in systemic glycemia. Further preclinical studies should evaluate ocular exposure, direct target engagement, functional visual outcomes, and reproducibility in larger cohorts.</jats:p>
title: Local RAGE Inhibition Attenuates Early Diabetic Retinal Pathology in Streptozotocin-Induced Rats

records.abstract: <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used as an intervention outcome; however, IC composites lack a standardized scoring method, hindering comparisons across trials. To determine whether the scoring method influenced the detection of intervention effects, we applied multiple composite scoring approaches to the same data and compared their responsiveness to a 12-week exercise intervention in older adults at risk of mild cognitive impairment. Methods: Pre- and post-intervention IC data were obtained from 59 community-dwelling older adults assigned to resistance training (n=34) or stretching and flexibility (n=25). The five-domain IC composite was computed repeatedly using alternative scoring approaches: z-score (concurrent and baseline-anchored variants), percentage of maximum possible (POMP), binary classification (0/1), and a three-category ordinal scale. Responsiveness was quantified using the standardized response mean (SRM). Results: Responsiveness ranged from negligible to large for identical data, indicating that the intervention effect depended on the scoring method. The ordinal and POMP composites were the most responsive (SRM 0.74–0.88 and 0.50–0.76). Within the z-score composite, responsiveness depended entirely on the standardization anchor: the concurrent specification was insensitive (SRM ≈ 0), whereas baseline-anchoring showed moderate responsiveness (0.62–0.71). The binary scoring was the least sensitive, showing a ceiling effect. Conclusions: Ordinal three-category scoring was the most responsive, suggesting that approaches combining a fixed reference with a category-based structure are well suited for detecting change in IC. This finding requires confirmation against external criteria for IC, such as its predictive validity for adverse health outcomes, along with domain weighting and instrument selection.</jats:p>
title: Toward Standardization of Intrinsic Capacity Assessment: A Methodological Comparison of the Responsiveness of Composite Scoring Methods

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as objective indicators of mobility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.06; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.13; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.14; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of objective impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Though exergames attract considerable research interest as tools for preserving cognitive function in older adults, a decade of meta-analytic evidence reveals a persistent gap between theoretical promise and empirical demonstration: exergames rarely outperform conventional motor-cognitive training and do not generate the sustained engagement that preventive benefit requires. These results reflect limitations that are structural: the field focused predominantly on clinical populations rather than primary prevention; training concepts borrowed from rehabilitation protocols rather than grounded in the specific neuroplastic mechanisms of the exergaming medium; and virtual environments that are digitally sophisticated but culturally and esthetically neutral, systematically excluding the stimulation that converging evidence from neuroaesthetics, cultural epidemiology, and narrative neuroscience identifies as a core active ingredient of brain health promotion. To address these limitations simultaneously, this viewpoint introduces Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) exergames, defined as “virtual reality solutions in which motor-cognitive interactions are embedded in artistic content, cultural heritage, or historically situated narrative to exploit optimal neurobiological substrates of the intervention.” Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework, we develop mutually reinforcing mechanistic pillars: multimodal sensorimotor engagement within ecologically valid immersive environments; semantic and narrative activation of memory systems; emotional and autobiographical resonance as a dopaminergic driver of learning consolidation and sustained participation; and the re-engineering of physical effort evaluation from aversive to appetitive through aesthetic pleasure and narrative absorption. A fundamental implication is that in MAGIC exergames, motivation is not engineered through gamification mechanics—it is released by the intrinsic value of inhabiting a culturally meaningful world. We further argue MAGIC exergames correspond to a specific use that is, Cultural Snacking, which consists of the serialization of MAGIC content into brief, narratively open daily episodes of 5 to 10 minutes, designed for 3 to 5 daily consumptions across varied contexts. This dosing architecture is compatible with the motivational profile of healthy older adults who do not identify as patients or trainees. The paper opens perspectives with a design and research agenda structured around three priorities: characterizing MAGIC exergames by the type of motor-cognitive interactions they deliver rather than by the technology platform; conducting mechanistic neuroimaging investigations targeting the specific biomarkers of neuroplastic benefit that creative cultural engagement is expected to produce; and building the intersectoral innovation ecosystem that brings cultural institutions, digital health teams, and older adults together as co-designers. Without waiting for MAGIC-specific trials, we invite the digital medicine, public health, and silver economy communities to recognize that museums, heritage sites, and cultural institutions are potentially the most ecologically valid, intrinsically motivating, and cost-effective substrates for a new generation of brain health exergames that are as meaningful as they are effective. The scientific, institutional, and economic conditions for this convergence already exist.</jats:p>
title: Rethinking the Prevention of Cognitive Decline in Healthy Older Adults: The Motor-Cognitive Active Gamified Immersive Cultural (MAGIC) Exergames

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Immersive virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used for embodied training, but its practical value for older adults depends on whether the experiential benefits can be achieved without unacceptable discomfort or overstated claims about motor learning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This randomized study compared head-mounted immersive VR with standardized, content-matched 2D video instruction for Tai Chi movement-encoding in community-dwelling older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 106 older adults were randomized to immersive VR (n=56) or video instruction (n=50). The primary analysis included 92 participants with complete age, pretest, and posttest data (VR: n=45; Video: n=47). The primary outcome was a 5-item movement-encoding knowledge score (range 0‐20), analyzed using analysis of covariance, with posttest score as the dependent variable and group, pretest score, and age as predictors. Secondary outcomes were intrinsic motivation, game experience, and learning engagement; safety, tolerability, and feasibility were assessed using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, Game Experience Questionnaire, Utrecht Work Engagement Scale–Short Form, participant flow, and Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire. VR system telemetry was analyzed descriptively as an exploratory process outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Adjusted posttest movement-encoding performance did not differ between VR and video instruction (adjusted difference −0.27, 95% CI −2.25 to 1.72;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.79; partial η
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      =0.001). The Game Experience Questionnaire results favored VR for competence (Video: mean 3.36, SD 1.21; VR: mean 4.15, SD 0.92;
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                      =0.009), flow (Video: mean 3.77, SD 1.26; VR: mean 4.46, SD 0.76;
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                      =0.014), and lower tension (Video: mean 1.76, SD 1.04; VR: mean 1.27, SD 0.63;
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                      =0.037), whereas challenge did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction (
                      <jats:italic>q</jats:italic>
                      =0.073). In the VR Group, recognition accuracy was associated with posttest movement-encoding score (n=44;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.317,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04), but pose accuracy was not (n=44;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.129,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.41). The Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire scores were low among valid VR participants (total score mean 3.77, SD 11.12), and 36 out of 46 (78%) participants reported zero symptoms.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>With a strong active control, immersive VR did not produce higher short-term Tai Chi movement-encoding performance than video instruction. Among participants who completed the VR session, the immediate game-experience profile was more favorable. These findings indicate that VR may offer experiential benefits, while also highlighting the need to manage cybersickness and technical exclusions and to distinguish movement knowledge from actual motor execution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Knowledge Performance, User Experience, and Cybersickness With Immersive Virtual Reality for Tai Chi Movement-Encoding in Older Adults: Randomized Comparison Study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Social disparities in oral health persist, disproportionately affecting Indigenous populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to compare oral health status, dental care access, treatment needs, and social determinants between Mapuche and non-Mapuche older adults in the La Araucanía Region of Chile, within a hybrid dental care model, and to explore whether ethnicity is associated with these outcomes, guided by the World Health Organization (WHO) Commission on Social Determinants of Health (CSDH) framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a cross-sectional exploratory analytic study using data from 480 adults aged 60 years or older who received dental care through a hybrid teledentistry and mobile clinic model (Geriatric Dental Specialties Tele-Platform [TEGO]) in 4 municipalities of La Araucanía. The analytic sample was restricted to community-dwelling, functionally independent older adults. Outcomes included oral health status (nonfunctional dentition, edentulism, cavitated caries, and periodontitis), dental care access (fixed prosthetic rehabilitation and unmet denture need), and dental treatment needs (restorative and prosthetic). Structural (sex, age, education, rurality, and ethnicity) and intermediary determinants (behavioral, biological, psychosocial, and health system access) were analyzed following the WHO-CSDH framework. Bivariate analyses compared outcomes between Mapuche and non-Mapuche participants. Multivariable logistic regression models examined associations between determinants and outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 471 older adults (mean age 72.8, SD 7.7 years) were included; 76.9% (362/471) had nonfunctional dentition, 18% (85/471) were edentulous, 25.6% (98/383) had cavitated caries, and 46% (154/335) had periodontitis. In bivariate analyses, Mapuche participants showed lower educational attainment, higher rural residence, poorer oral health, more behavioral risk factors (eg, infrequent toothbrushing and higher sugar intake), greater restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care compared with non-Indigenous peers. In multivariable analyses, female sex was associated with increased odds of edentulism but lower odds of periodontitis. Lower education was associated with nonfunctional dentition (odds ratio [OR] 4.28, 95% CI 2.34-7.88; P<.001) and edentulism (OR 3.04, 95% CI 1.52-6.09; P=.002). Mapuche ethnicity was associated with higher prevalence of cavitated caries (OR 2.40, 95% CI 1.25-4.63; P=.009) and periodontitis (OR 2.43, 95% CI 1.21-4.88; P=.01). Dental care access was associated with behavioral factors (brushing, interproximal hygiene, and sugar intake) and structural determinants (age, sex, and rurality), while restorative and prosthetic needs were linked to sugar consumption and tobacco use, respectively.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Oral health inequalities among older adults in La Araucanía were associated with both structural and behavioral determinants. Although Mapuche participants exhibited poorer oral health, higher restorative needs, and reduced access to complex dental care in bivariate analyses, ethnicity remained associated only with cavitated caries and periodontitis in adjusted models. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating social determinants into oral health planning for underserved older adults and highlight the potential utility of data generated through digitally supported territorial care models for informing equity-oriented oral health strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social Determinants and Oral Health Among Indigenous and Non-Indigenous Older Adults in La Araucanía, Chile: Cross-Sectional Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The phase angle (PhA) and extracellular water (ECW)–to–total body water (TBW) ratio serve as indicators of cell membrane integrity and body fluid balance in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined the domain-specific associations of physical activity (PA) with PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A nationally representative sample of 5211 adults aged 50 years and older was analyzed. Weekly amounts of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) in leisure-time, occupational, and transport-related domains were assessed using the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire. A bioelectrical impedance analyzer was used to measure PhA (°) and the ECW-to-TBW ratio (%). Linear regression analyses were conducted.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For leisure-time PA, compared with 0 min/week, participating in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with 0.08 (95% CI 0.02-0.14) and 0.13 (95% CI 0.06-0.20) degrees higher PhA, respectively. Additionally, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in 150 to 299 min/week and ≥300 min/week of MVPA was associated with –0.11 (95% CI –0.19 to –0.03) and –0.15 (95% CI –0.22 to –0.07) percentage points lower ECW-to-TBW ratio, respectively. For transport-related PA, compared with 0 min/week, engaging in ≥300 min/week of MVPA was negatively associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio (β=–0.07, 95% CI –0.14 to –0.01). Occupational PA showed no clear associations with PhA or the ECW-to-TBW ratio.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the observed associations were modest, the associations of PA with both PhA and the ECW-to-TBW ratio differed across PA domains. Specifically, leisure-time PA was positively associated with PhA and inversely associated with the ECW-to-TBW ratio. These findings highlight the potential role of leisure-time PA in improving bioelectrical markers of cellular health and fluid distribution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Domain-Specific Associations of Physical Activity With Phase Angle and Extracellular Water–to–Total Body Water Ratio in Middle-Aged or Older Adults: Cross-Sectional Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p &lt; 0.05). Stratified analyses showed that physical activity was positively associated with IC among females, urban residents, foreign-born participants, and US-born participants, while having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC across most subgroups. Among the interactions examined, only the association between physical activity and IC differed significantly by gender (p &lt; 0.05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Elder abuse and self-neglect (EASN) remain pervasive phenomena, yet intervention research is limited. Adult Protective Services (APS) plays a central role, but statutory timelines and resource constraints make long-term follow-up difficult. RISE was developed to fill this systems gap as a complement to APS, extending support beyond the investigative phase. Initial implementation of the RISE-APS model at the state level in Maine demonstrated feasibility, acceptability, and improvement in case outcomes. Building on these findings, the present study examines the pre-implementation phase of replicating this model in three new U.S. sites serving different communities to identify implementation determinants likely to shape integration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted six focus groups with 25 managers from APS and partnering community-based organizations housing RISE in three U.S. states. Transcripts underwent reflexive thematic analysis guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants noted strong philosophical compatibility between RISE and existing practices. However, structural constraints, including bureaucratic bottlenecks and APS staffing instability, could impede delivery. The warm handoff was viewed as central to engagement, yet sometimes unrealistic given resource constraints or limited time available to build APS-client rapport. Furthermore, while broad service networks may ease initial integration, dedicated partnership maintenance is required to sustain referral flow.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight the organizational conditions and partnership infrastructure necessary to support replication of the RISE-APS model. Feasibility relies not only on philosophical alignment but on adapting workflows to withstand turnover, resource limitations, and structural constraints across varying service systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Replicating the RISE-APS Elder Abuse and Self-Neglect Intervention Model in new contexts: A pre-implementation analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Chinese American family caregivers face cultural and logistical barriers to accessing dementia care services. This study evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, usability, and preliminary signals of benefit of a culturally and linguistically tailored, web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study used a two-phase design comprising usability and acceptability testing followed by a single-arm pre-post evaluation to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and usability of the decision aid among Chinese American family caregivers (N=74) who had provided care to a family member with dementia or dementia-related symptoms and to report preliminary outcomes on changes in dementia care knowledge and decisional conflict.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The decision aid demonstrated high acceptability and usability. All participants rated the length and informational content as appropriate, and the tool was perceived as easy to use, informative, and helpful for decision-making. Consistent with predefined progression criteria, significant improvements were observed in dementia care knowledge, particularly in home and long-term care. Decisional conflict was significantly reduced, reflecting greater understanding of care options, clearer perceptions of benefits and risks, and increased confidence in decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Decision-related outcomes improved following exposure, indicating greater clarity and confidence in decision-making. Findings suggest that this culturally and linguistically tailored decision aid met early-phase progression criteria for acceptability, usability, and improvement in proximal outcomes, supporting its advancement to the next phase of testing. Future research should evaluate behavioral and longer-term outcomes, all of which will be important for subsequent controlled trials.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: A culturally and linguistically tailored web-based decision aid for dementia care decision-making among Chinese American family caregivers: Feasibility and preliminary effects

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As cigarette smoking continues to decline among youth and young adults, smoking rates among older U.S. adults remain unchanged. Historically, cigarette and, more recently, e-cigarette tax policies influenced smoking behavior in younger smokers. This study examined how older smokers respond to tax changes to inform public health strategies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our data combined a panel of state cigarette and standardized e-cigarette tax rates with individual-level survey microdata. Our sample included adults aged ≥65, with and without a history of smoking. We estimated two-way fixed-effects population-weighted regression models of current smoking and past-year quit attempts. Exploratory subgroup analyses tested for heterogeneity by education and income level.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 3,117,382 adults, 48% had a history of smoking; of whom 18% currently smoked. A $1.00 cigarette tax increase was associated with current smoking: est. = -0.56 percentage points (pp) (CI: -0.85, -0.27). A $0.10 increase in e-cigarette tax (open) was associated with current smoking (+0.28 pp; CI: 0.01, 0.55). Approaching tax parity by one dollar was associated with a 0.48-pp (CI: 0.20, 0.76) increase in current smoking. While varied by socioeconomic status, there was no association between cigarette/e-cigarette taxes and quit attempts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For older U.S. adults, cigarette taxes were associated with lower smoking, whereas e-cigarette taxes were associated with higher smoking. The type of e-cigarette tax appears important for tobacco control in older smokers. Policies increasing the relative cost of e-cigarettes may perpetuate smoking rates in older populations at the highest risk of smoking-related harm.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Cigarette and e-cigarette tax effects on the oldest generation of smokers in the United States

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and “connected.”</jats:p>
title: Being sensed, scored, and “connected”: a social-gerontological critique of artificial intelligence-driven loneliness detection for older adults in Taiwan

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.</jats:p>
title: Vulnerability intersections: an integrative conceptual framework for understanding vulnerability in AI-assisted care for older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In many countries, population aging and increasing rates of housing security among older people are unfolding simultaneously. While the World Health Organization's Age-Friendly Cities and Communities (AFCC) framework is largely considered the leading framework for developing age-supportive communities, it does not adequately account for the ways in which a community may be inclusive, supportive, or age-friendly for older people with lived experience of housing insecurity. This paper began with a question: What would an age-friendly community look like for older people with experiences of housing insecurity? Drawing on the Aging in the Right Place (AIRP) framework, a rights-based conceptual model of six indicators developed through community-based participatory research, this paper re-examines and extends each of the WHO AFCC framework's eight domains: housing, transportation, social participation, respect and social inclusion, civic participation, communication and information, community support and health services, and outdoor spaces and buildings. This paper argues that age-friendly approaches must recognize housing as a human right and housing security as a cornerstone of age-friendly communities, requiring protections including rent control, eviction prevention, and incentives for non-market housing development. Recommendations are offered for municipalities seeking to embed AIRP and rights-based perspectives into age-friendly strategies and evaluation.</jats:p>
title: Re-Examining Age-Friendly Communities for Older People with Insecure Housing Histories

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Effective and sustainable support for family caregivers is a growing priority, yet practical guidance for scaling promising coaching interventions into routine practice is limited. The objective of this evaluation was to identify organizational determinants, barriers, facilitators, and adaptations affecting national implementation of the Caregiver Health and Wellbeing Coaching (CHWC) program in the Veterans Health Administration.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An explanatory, sequential mixed‑methods design included surveys of CHWC staff (n = 53) and qualitative interviews (n = 14), guided by the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research, its Outcomes Addendum, and the Framework for Reporting Adaptations and Modifications‑Enhanced.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Successful implementation—defined as program launch and delivery to at least one caregiver at each site—and successful sustainment—defined as ongoing or expanding delivery to new and returning caregivers—were associated with thorough planning, leadership engagement, and flexible delivery. Barriers included staff turnover, complex documentation, and challenges recruiting caregivers. Facilitators and process improvements were rapidly integrated into program operations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings can inform strategies to scale caregiver support programs that underpin sustainable aging and long-term care systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Scaling Caregiver Health and Wellbeing Coaching: A Mixed Methods Evaluation of Implementation and Sustainment in the Veterans Health Administration

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Disempowerment in the context of chronic illness refers to the state of dissatisfaction with diminishing opportunities to control personal lives, potentially leading to disengagement in health management and negative health outcomes. However, the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in chronic illness among older adults are not fully understood. This study aims to explore the experiences and perceptions of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Qualitative description was employed. From January to March 2025, individual face-to-face semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 Cantonese-speaking older adults with chronic illness. Template analysis was used.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three themes emerged regarding the experiences of disempowerment: (1) confusion and uncertainty amid unexpected changes and unclear information, (2) struggles to manage their health in the way they would like, and (3) difficulty in living the life they had before or had hoped for. Negative feelings towards the experiences were also identified with indirect expression to others. The causes included: (1) irreversibly declining health and intrinsic capacity, (2) unmet expectations, and (3) age discrimination. The consequences involved: (1) disengaging the context of disempowerment by suppressing negative emotions, distancing themselves from care partners, and trying to overcome the situation, followed by (2) accepting or despairing over time.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study revealed the experiences and perceptions, causes and consequences of disempowerment in older adults with chronic illness. The tendency to indirectly express or suppress the negative feelings underscores a need for tailored strategies to better assess and address disempowerment in this population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Exploring Experiences of Disempowerment in Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Study
