<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Little is known regarding the effects of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (AD/ADRD) in in American Indian and First Nation (AI/FN) communities in the US and Canada. Yet, research suggests FN populations in Canada experience 34% higher dementia rates and over half of US-based Indigenous adults demonstrate incident cognitive impairment, including dementia due to AD and/or cerebrovascular disease. Already higher than the general population, rates will increase as Indigenous populations age. The Indigenous Cultural Understandings of ADRD-Research and Engagement (ICARE) project was established to understand lived-experiences of dementia in AI/FN communities around the Great Lakes. We report themes describing practitioner experiences providing dementia care in selected US and Canadian Indigenous communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthcare practitioners (n = 14) providing care in Indigenous communities were interviewed by community-based researchers using semi-structured guides exploring a range of topics. Thematic analysis was used to identify challenges and recommendations to improve care. Trustworthiness checks included reflexivity, consensus, prolonged engagement, member checking and audit.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thematic analysis yielded six superordinate themes. Provider-perceived challenges included: 1) Limited Resources for Providing Dementia Care, 2) Need for Caregiver-focused Preparation and Support, 3) Communication and Relationship Gaps, 4) Low-levels of Community Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement. Provider recommendations were characterized as: 5) Increase Dementia-related Awareness, Education and Engagement, 6) Invest in Dementia Caregiver Support and Community Strengths.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings were contextualized with post-colonial and relational care frameworks. Providers described relevant challenges and provided culturally safe and equitable strategies to improve dementia care outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Healthcare Provider Experiences Delivering Dementia Care in Indigenous Communities: Challenges and Recommendations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The objective of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The goal of the Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol was to establish a comprehensive, nationally representative assessment of cognitive, physical, and sensory function in early midlife to support longitudinal and life course Alzheimer’s disease risk research. We developed the Add CAPS, a comprehensive and multidimensional assessment battery in Wave VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We describe protocol implementation and examine the distribution of cognitive, physical, and sensory measures by age, sex, and educational attainment in Add Health Wave VI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among participants who completed the survey, response rates were approximately 85% for digital cognitive assessments and 94% for interviewer-administered cognitive, physical, and hearing measures. Participants with complete Add CAPS data had a mean age of 44.2 years. Cognitive performance varied by age, education, and sex. Younger participants and those with higher educational attainment had better cognitive performance scores across assessments. Participants who were male, older, and had lower educational attainment had poorer hearing. There were no age differences in grip strength, but it did vary by educational attainment. Survey-reported cognitive and physical challenges were common.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Add CAPS Protocol fills a critical gap by providing robust measures of cognitive, physical, and sensory function earlier in the adult life course than most nationally representative aging studies. These data will support future research on aging trajectories and health in the U.S. population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Study design and results of the Wave VI Add Health Cognitive Assessment, Physical, and Sensory Function (Add CAPS) protocol

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We introduce comprehensive, multilevel, time-varying contextual indicators linked to the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), describe Black–White differences in their distributions and trends across the early life course, and provide methodological considerations for using these new data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Contextual indicators spanning housing and credit market, political, criminal-legal, cultural climate, and historical domains at various geographic levels were compiled from external data sources and merged to Add Health respondents’ state, county, census tract, and block group locations across Waves I–V (1994–2018), capturing exposures from adolescence (ages 12–20) through early midlife (ages 33–42). Descriptive statistics for each indicator—overall and by race (Black and White)—are presented alongside temporal trends.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Substantial and persistent Black–White disparities were observed across domains and waves. Relative to White respondents, Black respondents were more likely to reside in counties characterized by higher eviction rates, greater racialized economic segregation, elevated housing cost burden, higher incarceration rates, and more hate crime incidents. Black respondents also lived in states with greater historical lynching violence. Methodological considerations presented include data source-level characteristics (e.g., data collection procedures and coverage) and measure-specific considerations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By linking comprehensive place-based socio-contextual measures to Add Health’s rich biological, demographic, behavioral, and psychosocial data spanning critical developmental periods, and a new battery of cognitive, physical, and sensory function in midlife, researchers can identify life course pathways of aging inequalities and inform interventions to reduce trends and disparities in healthy aging in American society.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Novel place-based socio-contextual measures in Add Health for aging researchers: characteristics and methodological considerations

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the associations between educational characteristics and cognitive functioning among U.S. early midlife adults and to assess how biological sex modifies these associations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data on up to 9,420 participants from Waves I–VI of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), we assessed the association between education (degree attained and secondary school features) and cognitive functioning (working memory, episodic memory, executive function, processing speed, and language/fluency) at midlife (ages 39 to 51 years) with linear regression. We adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, measures of adolescent cognition (baseline Add Health Picture Vocabulary Test), and social origins to minimize confounding of the exposure-outcome relationship. We further examined the interaction between degree attained and secondary school features and these associations stratified by biological sex. Weights for the complex Add Health sampling design were applied to ensure nationally representative results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher educational attainment was consistently associated with better midlife cognition, as measured by the composite TestMyBrain cognition score. Associations generally followed dose-response patterns by degree attained. In contrast, school feature measures were largely not associated with midlife cognition, and effect sizes were inconsistent when present. Sex-stratified analyses revealed similar patterns across sexes, though associations between education and some working memory and language measures were stronger among men, while associations with some episodic memory measures were stronger among women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Educational attainment is strongly associated with cognitive functioning in midlife, after adjustment for adolescent cognitive performance and social origins.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Educational attainment, secondary school features, and midlife cognitive functioning: understanding the associations between education and cognitive domains

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective age is a construct that displays considerable individual variability. This study, conducted within the Chinese context, investigates how major life events affect older adults’ subjective age, measured by felt age and look age, and the moderating effects of chronological age and community services for older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used a nationally representative sample of older adults aged 60 and over from three waves (collected in 2018, 2020, and 2023) of the China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey. Fixed-effects models were employed to examine how negative events (e.g., serious illness or death of a relative/friend) and positive events (e.g., a child’s marriage or childbearing) impact subjective age. Random-effects models were conducted for robustness checks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that experiencing negative events is associated with an older subjective age by approximately 1.3% or 1 year. In contrast, witnessing positive events reduces their felt age and look age by roughly 0.9% or 0.6 years and 1.2% or 0.9 years, respectively. The negative impact of adverse events on subjective age intensifies with chronological age, whereas the rejuvenating effect of positive events attenuates. The availability of community services for older adults significantly reduces the impact of both negative and positive life events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results highlight the complex relationship between life events and subjective age, suggesting that supportive environments can buffer older adults from the psychological effects of life transitions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Feeling younger or older? How life events reshape subjective age among Chinese older adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive aging is shaped by biological and social processes that unfold across the life course and the contexts in which they occur. Retirement may coincide with faster cognitive decline. Because cognitively supportive resources differ across places, this study assesses whether residential context (urban, suburban, rural/ex-urban) moderates cognitive trajectories before and after retirement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study (2000-2020; n = 3,675). We estimated within-person change in cognition before and after retirement and included interaction terms to test modification by residential context. To reduce compositional differences across contexts, we applied inverse probability of treatment weighting and estimated piecewise linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive decline was observed before and after retirement, with faster decline following retirement. Post-retirement decline was steepest in rural areas (-0.194 points/year), followed by suburban (-0.184) and urban (-0.164) settings. Pairwise contrasts indicated steeper post-retirement decline in rural than urban areas (β = -0.031 points/year), or 0.31 points over 10 years; urban-suburban differences were small. Results were similar after combining urban and suburban respondents.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retirement may represent a turning point during which geographic inequalities in cognitive aging widen. Faster post-retirement decline in rural contexts may reflect reduced access to social, environmental, and institutional resources, but these pathways were not directly tested and should be interpreted as plausible explanations. Findings point to the potential importance of place-based strategies to mitigate spatial disparities in cognitive aging among retirees.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Residential context and cognitive aging: Differences by urbanicity across the retirement transition

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As longitudinal panel surveys face escalating costs, many are transitioning from traditional in-person interviews to mixed-mode designs. While essential for fiscal sustainability, this shift creates a methodological challenge: distinguishing genuine longitudinal change from measurement effects introduced by the change in mode. This study evaluated the impact of this transition within the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) as the cohort entered midlife.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Utilizing Wave VI data and a randomized split-sample design (in which the eligible sample was randomly divided between a new web-first mixed-mode protocol [Sample 1] and an in-person control replicating the legacy survey protocol [Sample 2]), the study estimated the differential mode effect, capturing cross-sectional differences between the two designs. Subsequently, a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) was applied across Waves III–VI to decompose these design effects into mode-specific measurement error and residual nonresponse components.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Concerns regarding systemic declines in data quality were largely unfounded; the mixed-mode design outperformed the traditional in-person design in measurement accuracy. However, significant mode effects were identified for some items, particularly sensitive health outcomes and stigmatized behaviors, driven by distinct combinations of measurement error and differential nonresponse.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Because these differences can inadvertently mimic or obscure actual aging trends, researchers should screen variables for mode sensitivity and incorporate appropriate adjustments, such as a mode or design indicator, inverse propensity weighting, or HMM-based decomposition, in longitudinal analyses, ensuring that “signals” of aging are not obscured by survey redesign.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mode effects for Add Health in transition from in-person to mixed mode

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines associations between completed parity, including childlessness (zero parity), and a range of medical conditions (individually and cumulatively) and self-rated health, including differences associated with race/ethnicity-related factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conduct correlational and multivariable regression analyses using a historical HRS/AHEAD sample of ever-married, non-Hispanic Black and White women born between 1920 and 1941. Multivariable models adjust for early-life-course social determinants of health, including contextual birthplace exposure to Jim Crow-era structural racial inequalities. We focus on childlessness/zero parity by using zero-inflated count regression methods that statistically identify women with zero probability of having had a live birth (a latent “always-zero” group).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Black women had three times the odds of “always-zero” group membership and, if not in that group, an expected parity 11% higher than White women. In correlational analyses, the predicted probability of “always-zero” group membership (Predicted Infecundity Probability or PIP)—rather than reported childlessness status—and high parity were associated with high-fatality medical conditions and self-rated fair/poor health. In multivariable models, PIP and high parity were positively associated with number of conditions, while PIP and number of conditions were positively associated with self-rated fair/poor health. Net of parity, consistent with weathering, younger Black women had a higher-than-expected number of medical conditions relative to all women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In the context of historical structural racial inequality, race/ethnicity-related differences in childlessness and high parity were strongly associated with later-life, post-reproductive health disparities. Women’s number of births was associated with the accumulation of medical conditions in a U-shaped pattern.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Race/ethnicity, completed parity, and women’s later-life health in the Health and Retirement Study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective survival probability (SSP) is a key predictor of economic and health decisions in later life, yet existing research assumes that gains and losses in survival expectations have symmetric behavioral effects. This study examines how within-person changes in SSP are associated with health-promoting behaviors among middle-aged and older adults in South Korea.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using ten waves of the Korean Longitudinal Study of Ageing (2006-2024), we estimate individual fixed-effects models on an analytic sample of 65,069 person-wave observations from 10,878 individuals aged 45 and older. We extend the standard symmetric model by adopting an asymmetric fixed-effects framework, which decomposes cumulative SSP increases and decreases into separate parameters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The symmetric model shows that a one-unit increase in SSP (on a 0-10 scale) is associated with a 0.69 percentage-point increase in regular exercise, after controlling for self-rated health, chronic diseases, functional limitations, and socioeconomic characteristics. The asymmetric decomposition reveals two distinct patterns: exercise responds exclusively to SSP losses (loss-only), while paid health checkups respond only to SSP gains (gain-only). Formal symmetry tests reject equal absolute effects for both outcomes (p &lt; .05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings provide evidence that associations between changing survival expectations and health behaviors may be asymmetric. The domain-specific nature of these asymmetries—loss-only disengagement in exercise and gain-only investment in preventive care—suggests that interventions targeting middle-aged and older adults may benefit from considering potentially different mechanisms linking survival expectations to behavior across outcome domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Asymmetric behavioral responses to changes in subjective survival expectations: Implications for health investment in later life

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We examined the strength of intergenerational associations between midlife adults in Add Health and their Baby Boomer parents from the Add Health Parent Study (AHPS) across numerous substantive domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using linked data from AHPS Phase 1 (2015–2017), a subset of parents of Add Health respondents, with new Add Health Wave VI data, we estimated intergenerational correlations between each cohort’s socioeconomic status (e.g., income, economic insecurity, and educational attainment); family context (e.g., union formation, time/money transfers, and psychological traits); health (e.g., mental, physical, and behavioral); and life experiences (e.g., social integration). We harmonized measures across the two generations and estimated either Pearson (r) or polychoric (ρ) correlations depending on the level of measurement. Intergenerational correlations were further contrasted by sex, the biological relationship of the parent-child dyad, and educational attainment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The largest correlations were found within socioeconomic and health domains, with significant correlations found for food insecurity (ρ = 0.52), educational attainment (r = 0.42), diabetes (ρ = 0.41), and obesity (ρ = 0.37). We found more significant and larger correlations for biological parent-child dyads and parent-daughter dyads. Few educational grades in intergenerational correlations were significant (e.g., health behavior and social integration).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intergenerational correlations are stronger when there is a known shared genetic component in outcomes such as health and health behavior, but shared environments also play an important role for socioeconomic outcomes. Intergenerational similarities in advantage for the higher educated and disadvantage for the less educated are evident. Small sample sizes precluded analysis by race/ethnicity; however, AHPS Phase 2 data (2026–2027) will fill that research gap.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intergenerational differences and similarities in economic well-being, family context, health, and life experiences among older adult parents and their middle-aged children: data from the Add Health and Add Health Parent Studies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Gerontological and population health sciences increasingly emphasize life-course, biosocial frameworks linking social environments to biological aging and disease processes, for which high-quality biological data are essential. We report on the collection, assay, and quality of aging-related biomarkers in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) Waves V and VI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Staff collected blood specimens during in-home health exams, processed them locally, and shipped them to the lab for further processing, assay completion, and archiving. Analytes assessed cardiovascular disease risk, glucose homeostasis, lipids, renal function, hepatic injury, inflammation, immune system processes, and neurodegeneration. Inter-assay coefficients of variation (CVs) were estimated for sample sets. In 2% of participants, a duplicate specimen was collected within 2 weeks and assays repeated; intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were calculated to assess short-term reliability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wave V collected blood from 92% of 5,381 participants who completed the exam (mean age 38); Wave VI collected blood from 91% of 6,073 participants (mean age 44). Reliability was excellent (ICC ≥ 0.75) and highest for hemoglobin A1c at Waves V–VI and GFAP and HSV and SARS-CoV-2 serologies at Wave VI. Reliability was fair to good (ICC 0.40 to &lt;0.75) for assays of low-abundance proteins reflecting temporally dynamic biological processes; none were poor (ICC &lt; 0.40). CVs were desirable (&lt;10%) for established clinical chemistry assays but less so (≥10%) for low-abundance proteins, markers of temporally dynamic biological processes, and SARS-CoV-2.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-quality biological data from Add Health Waves V and VI greatly expand the study’s capacity to support life-course, biosocial research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Laboratory methods and quality assurance in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health Waves V and VI

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper describes the history and previous research contributions of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) and provides an overview of the recently completed Wave VI (average age 44 years) design and content. We provide a comparison of basic Wave VI data with two major U.S. cross-sectional health studies. We then report descriptive distributions for several survey-based health measures in Wave VI, both for the overall cohort as well as for subgroups. Finally, we discuss ways that Add Health data can be used to make important contributions to the study of health and aging in the U.S. population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wave VI utilized a mixed-mode (web and in-person) survey design, with follow-up home examinations to collect biological data. Using weighted Wave VI survey data, we provide descriptive distributions of selected early midlife health measures by race/ethnicity, educational attainment, and sex.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wave VI yielded 11,979 surveys, 6,073 home examinations, and thousands of contextual, environmental, and administrative variables. Self-reported survey data demonstrate the cohort’s relatively poor health, including nearly one-half with a body mass index above 30 kg/m2 and 17% reporting current depression. There are wide disparities by race/ethnicity and educational attainment in every assessed health outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wave VI of Add Health broke new ground in transforming a study of U.S. adolescents and young adults into a study of early midlife adults. These rich longitudinal, multi-level (i.e., social, biological, and contextual), nationally representative data are a key resource for understanding health and aging in American society.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Add Health becomes an aging study: conceptualization, history and Wave VI design, response, and descriptive health data

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults face prescriptive expectations about aging, including active aging norms emphasizing physical activity, social engagement, and autonomy. While previous research has linked active aging norms to health-related and social behaviors, no studies to date have examined whether and how these norms are related to proactive, future-oriented behaviors such as late-life preparation. Drawing on theories of norm internalization, this study examines self-attributed responsibility for aging preparation as a mediator linking active aging norms to late-life preparation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were drawn from the Ageing as Future project and included 1,003 participants aged 34 to 90 years (M = 58.82 years; 52% female). Late-life preparation was assessed using two complementary indicators: a count-based checklist of concrete preparatory behaviors and a continuous scale of perceived preparatory engagement. Mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS models, with Poisson regression-based mediation applied to the behavioral count outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across both indicators, stronger endorsement of active aging norms was associated with greater engagement in late-life preparation. These associations were partially mediated by perceived responsibility, indicating that individuals endorsing active aging norms more strongly were more likely to perceive preparation as their own responsibility, which was itself associated with higher preparatory engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that active aging norms are associated with late-life preparation in part through a greater sense of personal obligation to manage one’s own aging process, highlighting the role of norm internalization and perceived responsibility in translating prescriptive views of aging into proactive behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Internalizing active aging norms: Self-attributed responsibility as a mediator linking prescriptive views on aging to late-life preparation

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intensified immigration enforcement is a salient feature of contemporary U.S. sociopolitical environments with implications for healthy aging. This study examines whether immigration arrest rates are associated with working memory in early midlife and whether associations vary across ethnoracial groups.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using longitudinal data from The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, we assessed associations between county-level Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest rates and working memory measured via backward digit span recall at Wave VI. ICE rates were operationalized as the average number of arrests per 1,000 foreign-born adults in the prior year and linked to respondents’ county of residence at Wave V. Poisson regression models estimated associations across ethnoracial groups, with stratified analyses among Latinx and Asian respondents. Sensitivity analysis using multiple imputation assessed robustness to missing data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Latinx respondents residing in counties with higher ICE arrest rates exhibited significantly lower backward digit span recall relative to White respondents. No such associations were observed among Black or Asian respondents. The association was observed among U.S.-born Latinx respondents, and there was no evidence of nativity differences, but statistical power to detect those differences was limited. Sensitivity analyses produced similar results.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggest that immigration enforcement environments may be unevenly related to cognitive functioning across ethnoracial groups and that these associations may extend to U.S.-born members of racialized communities. By establishing a midlife cognitive benchmark, this study provides a foundation for future research on the relationship between immigration enforcement contexts and cognitive aging trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Immigration arrests and midlife cognitive health in the United States

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Recent trends of increasing midlife morbidity and mortality and widening educational disparities in the United States are concerning. This study documented the age pattern and educational disparities in health in the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) cohort as they enter midlife, and situates the cohort relative to preceding, similar, and following cohorts in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from Add Health and NHANES on 6 birth cohorts observed from adolescence to middle age, we characterized age patterns in general health, mental health, health behaviors, and chronic conditions within and across cohorts. We documented disparities by educational attainment, focusing on those with and without a 4-year college degree, and how such disparities emerge and evolve across the life course.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis showed that general health, mental health, and chronic disease deteriorated for the Add Health cohort as they aged into midlife, while health behaviors improved. Compared to the NHANES cohorts, the Add Health cohort had worse health than older cohorts, generally worse health compared to the same birth cohort, with some exceptions, and mixed health compared to younger cohorts. Educational gradients were relatively stable across age, with some evidence of increases, while educational gradients generally increased across cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The worsening health of the Add Health cohort with age and relative to previous cohorts has important implications for aging, as this currently midlife cohort of U.S. adults will enter old age in worse health than their predecessors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Midlife in crisis? Life course pathways to health at midlife across U.S. cohorts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Homebound status refers to needing assistance or an assistive device to leave home, being normally unable to leave home, or experiencing leaving home as a major effort. This study examines transitions into and out of homeboundness and whether family structure is associated with these transitions, with attention to gender differences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using National Health and Aging Trends Study data from 2011–2024, transition probabilities across four states—independent, homebound, nursing home residence, and deceased—were estimated using an unadjusted continuous-time homogeneous Markov model. Multinomial logistic regression models then assessed associations between family structure and subsequent transitions, including gender interactions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among respondents who were independent, 84.6% remained independent, and 12.2% became homebound by the next wave. Among those who were homebound, 23.6% returned to independence, 60.1% remained homebound, 2.4% entered nursing home residence, and 13.9% died. Unpartnered older adults had higher risks of transitioning from independence to nursing home (RRR = 1.752, p &lt;.01) and death (RRR = 1.265, p &lt;.01). Parents had lower risks than childless older adults of transitioning from independence to nursing home (RRR = 0.523, p &lt;.01) and death (RRR = 0.735, p &lt;.01), and from homeboundness to nursing home (RRR = 0.574, p &lt;.001). The association between being unpartnered and becoming homebound was significantly stronger among men than women.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>: Homeboundness as a dynamic and socially structured process. Family structure may shape pathways into homeboundness, institutional care, and death, with implications for aging in place.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Family structure and transitions into and out of homeboundness: Evidence from the National Health and Aging Trends Study, 2011–2024

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>U.S.-based Latino older adult populations face disproportionate barriers to accessing behavioral health services. We examined associations between multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking from different sources of behavioral health supports among understudied Latino older adults with behavioral health problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data come from a cross-sectional survey that included U.S.-based Latino residents ages 50-86 (N=274; 2021). The survey measured mental illness biopsychosocial causal beliefs, treatment efficacy beliefs, and social rejection beliefs as multiple facets of mental illness stigma that may influence mental and physical health help-seeking behaviors from four sources: traditional media, online/digital media, family/friends, and healthcare providers. Linear regression models examined associations between each stigma component and each help-seeking outcome, adjusting for personal/family factors in the full sample of Latino older adults and among a subsample reporting a self/familial behavioral health problem (n=173).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among Latino older adults with self/familial behavioral health problems, higher biopsychosocial causal beliefs were associated with increased mental and physical health help-seeking from healthcare providers (p&lt;0.05), while social rejection beliefs were associated with decreased mental/physical health help-seeking from healthcare providers (p&lt;0.05). Similarly, higher biopsychosocial causal beliefs were associated with increased mental health help-seeking from traditional media (p&lt;0.05) among those with self/familial behavioral health problems. No associations were observed between stigma components and mental/physical health help-seeking from online media or family/friends. Similar results, though attenuated, were found in the full sample.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multifaceted anti-stigma interventions for multi-generational Latino families may be an opportune strategy for increasing help-seeking for behavioral health problems among Latino older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Multifaceted mental illness stigma and help-seeking behaviors among Latino older adults experiencing behavioral health problems

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to better understand the effect of social disconnection on cognitive aging regarding its life course variation, temporal dynamics, and multidimensionality.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted coordinated data analysis of three large U.S. population-based longitudinal cohort panels (Add Health I–VI, MIDUS 1–3, and HRS 2006–2020) consisting of 18,553 individuals aged 11+. We harmonized measures of longitudinal patterns of social isolation and loneliness (never/transient/persistent), episodic memory (word recalls), and working memory (backward digit span and serial 7’s) across datasets. We estimated growth curve models to assess prospective associations of social isolation and loneliness with subsequent memory trajectories from adolescence to old adulthood.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We found strong detrimental effects of social isolation in both young and older adulthood and loneliness in older adulthood on memory function. Longer (particularly persistent) exposures to isolation and loneliness predicted poorer memory test scores. These effects were attenuated but largely remained significant after adjusting for sociodemographic, behavioral, and health risk factors. Social isolation and loneliness show weaker and less consistent associations with the rate of memory decline across the life course samples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Comparative life course research helped to elucidate the complex relationship between social disconnection and memory change and inform the timing and duration of cognitive impacts of objective and subjective social disconnection. Interventions to promote healthy aging should focus on reducing the chronicity of isolation starting early in life and feelings of loneliness in later life. Future research should include additional longitudinal data to further investigate links between cognition, social disconnection, and underlying mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Social disconnection and cognitive aging across the life course: coordinated longitudinal analysis of three national cohort studies

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined family and neighborhood conditions in adolescence and subsequent mortality over 29 years for a cohort of individuals recently reaching middle age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We employed a nationally representative sample of adolescents (N = 18,921) from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). Survey and linked contextual data from Wave I (1994–1995) offered information on conditions in adolescence (ages 12–19), and the Add Health Mortality Outcomes Surveillance Study (Add Health MOSS) provided mortality follow-up through the end of 2023.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cox proportional hazard models revealed that adolescents in lower socioeconomic status (SES) families and neighborhoods with greater concentrated disadvantage had increased all-cause mortality from adolescence through midlife. These family and neighborhood measures were attenuated when accounting for one another and were further diminished when controlling for individual-level factors reflecting adolescent development, particularly cognitive skills and educational expectations. Neighborhood disadvantage showed stronger results for external causes, whereas low parental education displayed a more robust relationship with internal causes of death.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings support the long arm of childhood perspective in highlighting the importance of adolescent conditions for subsequent mortality up to midlife. The association between neighborhood concentrated disadvantage and mortality points to residential context as an important early life exposure for further research. Family SES, neighborhood disadvantage, and individual aptitude and motivation together influence the risk of death in adulthood. Our study contributes to a better understanding of individual, family, and neighborhood contexts in adolescence, which can ultimately improve aging and lengthen lives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Family and neighborhood environments in adolescence and subsequent mortality

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mental health is a central concern for aging and well-being over the life course. This study examined ethno-racial patterns of depressive symptoms and loneliness among a diverse cohort of U.S. midlife adults to illuminate why some individuals age more successfully than others. Drawing on the Stress Process Model, we investigated whether these patterns persist after accounting for socioeconomic and relational stressors and social support resources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used new Wave VI data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). Descriptive statistics and negative binomial regression were employed to document ethno-racial variation in depressive symptoms and loneliness among this cohort of midlife U.S. adults (N = 11,435; ages 39–50).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multiracial adults initially reported slightly higher depressive symptoms and loneliness relative to White adults, but these differences were attenuated with adjustment for stressors and social support. Black adults exhibited poorer mental health than White adults descriptively, but better outcomes after adjusting for stressors and social support. Hispanic adults reported lower levels of depressive symptoms and loneliness than White adults net of sociodemographic covariates. Asian adults demonstrated no statistically significant differences from White adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ethno-racial groups each display unique mental health patterns in midlife, possibly reflecting differences in how ethno-racial groups perceive and cultivate resources in response to stressors and adverse structural conditions. Future studies should continue to investigate the complex set of factors which shape the mental well-being and aging of the U.S. population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: The ethno-racial patterning of depression and loneliness: new evidence from a diverse cohort of U.S. midlife adults

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Latent Structures of Social Determinants of Health in Later Life: A Comparison of U.S.-Born and Immigrants

                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigated the associations between control beliefs and the emotional aspects of psychological frailty (i.e., depression, anxiety, and loneliness) among older married couples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Multivariate Actor-Partner Interdependence Models were used to analyze data from 538 couples aged 65 or older, drawn from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Individuals’ own control beliefs were consistently associated with lower levels of depression, anxiety, and loneliness for both spouses. A partner effect emerged for loneliness, with wives’ control beliefs associated with lower levels of loneliness in their husbands, but this was not significant after adjusting for marital support and strain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings identify control beliefs as a consistent individual-level protective factor. Interventions to improve emotional well-being in older couples should prioritize strengthening personal control beliefs. Dyadic processes merit further investigation, particularly for outcomes such as loneliness that are closely embedded in the relational context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Control Beliefs and Emotional Aspects of Psychological Frailty Among Couples in Later Life

records.abstract: <jats:p>To assess whether national reductions in antipsychotic prescribing in U.S. nursing homes were shared equitably or masked widening gaps between top and bottom performers, we examined distributional trends across facilities from 2013 to 2023 using national facility-level data (CMS Provider Data Catalog; LTCFocus). We modeled long-stay antipsychotic measure performance using linear quantile mixed regression, assessed mobility across performance quartiles with transition matrices, and evaluated facility characteristics associated with trajectories. From 2013 to 2019, prescribing fell across all quantiles, with the steepest reductions among the worst performers, narrowing gaps with the best. After 2020, progress diverged: lower-performing facilities experienced sharp setbacks while top performers maintained gains. Mobility analyses showed entrenched disadvantage, with bottom-quartile facilities disproportionately likely to remain there. Higher Medicaid share predicted decline, whereas higher star ratings predicted improvement. The pandemic reversed earlier equity gains, amplifying structural disparities and exposing unequal capacity to sustain improvement.</jats:p>
title: Structural Vulnerability and the Pandemic: Widening Gaps in Nursing Home Antipsychotic Prescribing

                    <jats:p>Social isolation and loneliness in later life are major public health concerns associated with increased morbidity and premature mortality. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) constitute the primary local infrastructure for aging services in the US.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>

                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Most AAAs offered multiple social engagement programs; volunteer engagement (66.0%), arts and creative activities (62.2%), visiting/calling programs (57.7%), and technology engagement (55.5%) were common. Non-rural AAAs were more likely to offer visiting/calling, technology-based activities, and memory cafes, while rural AAAs were more likely to partner with public health units. records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.</jats:p>
title: Ageism and Quality of Life in Older Adults: The Roles of Self-Disgust and Psychological Distress

records.abstract: <jats:p>Smartphone addiction risk is an underexamined concern in later life, and prior research often treats older adults as a homogeneous group. Using cross-sectional survey data from 2,275 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older in Guangzhou, this exploratory study applied XGBoost with SHAP analysis to identify predictive correlates, followed by K-means clustering to examine subgroup heterogeneity among participants classified as high risk. Social participation and depressive symptoms were associated with the risk with nonlinear patterns. Two exploratory profiles were identified: the Socially Active profile (40.7%), characterized by high participation and more regular non-kin contacts, and the Emotionally Withdrawn profile (59.3%), characterized by elevated depressive symptoms, fewer regular non-kin contacts, and entertainment-oriented use. The findings lend credence to the paradigms of social overload and emotional compensation and suggest that digital inclusion among older adults must be coupled with support for digital self-regulation, psychological well-being, and social and family engagements.</jats:p>
title: Exploring Heterogeneity in Smartphone Addiction Risk Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults in Guangzhou: A Machine Learning Analysis

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates the impact of long-term care insurance (LTCI) on older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Using national representative data from four waves of CHARLS (2011, 2013, 2015, 2018), we find that LTCI decreases older adults’ monthly outpatient visits but is associated with an increase in both annual inpatient stays and inpatient medical expenses. Further evidence suggests that older adults covered by the pilot LTCI program have better health status compared to their counterparts in non-pilot cities. Overall, findings offer empirical support for the role of the LTCI program in Chinese older adults’ hospital service utilization, medical expenses, and health. Findings of China’s LTCI may offer insights for other countries with a large aging population but with no feasible LTCI framework.</jats:p>
title: Does the Pilot Long-Term Care Insurance Work as Expected in China? Examining its Impact on Hospital Utilizations, Medical Expenses, and Health

records.abstract: <jats:p>Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person (MFP) Program enables nursing home residents to return to community living, yet people living with dementia (PLWD) less often transition to the community through MFP, for unclear reasons. To understand mechanisms underlying this disparity, we conducted in-depth interviews with 44 older adults in Connecticut eligible for MFP and 44 family caregivers (41% PLWD/PLWD family members). Desire to move, program awareness, ability to self-advocate, personal care needs, family support, housing and home and community-based services (HCBS) resources all influenced moves. PLWD less often desired to move, typically required more assistance to move, were less able to self-advocate and manage logistics, had higher personal care needs, needed more family/informal support, and had additional safety and supervision needs. Better support for PLWD is needed in transition and HCBS programs as the population grows, nursing homes beds decrease, and the desire to live in the community persists.</jats:p>
title: “I Wanted to Get Back Out There”: In-depth Interviews With Older Adults and Family Caregivers About Moving Out of Nursing Homes Using Medicaid’s Money Follows the Person Program and How Dementia Influences Transitions

records.abstract: <jats:p>The adoption of care robots for older adult care is often framed as a question of whether older adults will accept the technology. This paper argues that, in family-based care for older adults at home, an equally important question is how adult children position care robots within intergenerational care relationships and their responsibility for ageing parents. Using Q methodology with 42 Chinese only children, by-person factor analysis identified four profiles: the Worried Controller, who may prioritise safety over parental autonomy; the Modern Filial, who sees tailored robots as a contemporary expression of filial piety; the Presence Keeper, who resists technologies that substitute for family presence; and the Filial Complementarity Conditionalist, who sees robots as supplementary to filial and emphasises broader policy and service conditions. These profiles show how participants balance filial obligation, caregiving pressure, parental autonomy, family presence, and wider conditions surrounding care-robot use.</jats:p>
title: Positioning Care Robots Within Filial Responsibility: Perspectives of Chinese Only Children

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines age differences in memories for a fictional story. We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. In the young listener condition, 35 older and 37 young adults recalled the episode to a young adult. In the older listener condition, 40 older and 37 young participants recalled it to an older adult. Memories were analyzed with three complementary methods: (1) a measure of episodic specificity, (2) a quantification of semantic similarity, and (3) the lexical content. Results revealed that young adults had more similar memories than older adults, and used more words related to negative emotions than older adults. However, older adults recalled as many episodic details as younger participants. There was no difference as a function of the recipient's age. Overall, these results underscore the value of studying memory in everyday social contexts.</jats:p>
title: Age Effects in Story Recall: Comparing the Narrative Similarities of Memories for a Fictional Movie

records.abstract: <jats:p>Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. This study examined younger and older adults’ perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare during COVID-19 through a social identity approach. Using a story completion method, 22 older and 41 younger adult participants completed a story about a younger or older COVID-19 patient and doctors allocating the last available ventilator. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death. Results support the need for policies protecting against the influence of ageism in healthcare systems and emphasise the need to understand how internalised ageism may influence perceptions and health behaviours of older patients.</jats:p>
title: Understandings of Ageism and Healthcare in the COVID-19 Pandemic

records.abstract: <jats:p>In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.</jats:p>
title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework

                    To map the evidence of disparities in cognition across different social determinants of health (SDOH), examine how SDOH are measured in the context of research on cognitive outcomes and identify knowledge gaps. PubMed, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched. We included peer-reviewed studies of adults that examined SDOH as primary exposures in relation to cognitive outcomes, and described a SDOH framework or definition in the context of cognition. Non-human studies, case reports, case series, editorials, protocols, and abstract-only records were excluded. Ninety-one records were included. Most of the included studies were conducted in the US and the most frequently used framework was the

Most of the existing research failed to explain the concept of SDOH and lacked a framework to guide the inclusion and interpretation of SDOH indicators. SDOH measures were heterogeneous across studies, with many examining only a single indicator and limited use of multidimensional approaches. This heterogeneity made findings challenging to compare. More research is needed on multidimensional SDOH and cognition in various racial/ethnic groups and less-studied geographic and cultural contexts, under explicit SDOH frameworks.

records.abstract: <jats:p>In the context of global demographic change, the number of patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other forms of dementia is steadily increasing. These individuals require ongoing care but often struggle to communicate their needs and preferences regarding quality care. This study re-examines existing qualitative data to explore perceptions of “quality care” for patients with AD within the Turkish sociocultural context. Building on a primary study of caregivers’ definitions of quality care, it employs a secondary analysis approach to generate new insights without collecting additional data. The dataset includes face-to-face, semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 15 formal and informal caregivers, including family members, professional caregivers, and managers from care institutions across four provinces in Türkiye. Analysis reveals that patients with AD often experience discomfort when their bodies are exposed or touched, particularly in ways that infringe upon their sense of privacy. Caregivers emphasised that protecting privacy relies on understanding the individual’s life story, values, and preferences, highlighting the role of relational familiarity in delivering care. Many participants described forming close, family-like bonds, often adopting kinship roles to provide personalised support. These dynamics were also shaped by gender norms, with caregiving commonly framed through a mother-child lens, reflecting societal expectations that women assume primary caregiving responsibilities. The findings show how privacy, emotional closeness, and gender roles intersect to shape caregiving practices. These findings suggest that care quality for patients with AD in Türkiye may be enhanced by approaches that attend to cultural and relational dimensions, recognise caregiver support needs, and incorporate culturally attuned practices — though further research across diverse settings is needed to assess the broader applicability of these insights. These insights contribute to the international discourse on dementia care by showing how culturally specific practices can guide globally relevant approaches to quality care.</jats:p>
title: Caregiver Perspectives on Alzheimer’s Care in the Turkish Sociocultural Context

records.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population
